table.text: To ask whether the variability of memorability itself was reduced, we estimated the reliability-corrected variance of concept memorability on the 559 concepts tested in both sets: participants were split at random into two halves (200 splits), concept corrected recognition was computed from the pooled trials of each half, and the covariance of the two halves' values across concepts, to which trial-to-trial noise does not contribute, was averaged over splits.
Thus, we strongly believe future memorability studies should use a more standard study-test design or at minimum ensure participants are reliably above floor on false alarm rates.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.expanded: However, in line with the general structure of global matching models, we found items that are more similar to other items in aggregate (summed similarity of raw feature representations, not differentiating by rare vs. common features as REM does) have greater interference in matching and thus worse memory performance (memorability vs. summed similarity to all other items across all of the features: r = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.52], p < 0.01; Fig. 1a).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2370 columns across 231 data files.
#### Issues Identified

100 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 231 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All experiments reported here were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before taking part.
live_data_statements: In addition, when we gave a global matching model the same study lists and test trials that our participants saw, it reproduced the inversion of Fig. 1c and correctly predicted that an image would be better remembered in the image set where it was more distinctive (SI Appendix, Section 8).
The relationship between summed similarity and memorability, at the level of both concepts and features, also did not depend on our participant exclusion criteria (SI Appendix, Section 1).
All experiments reported here were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before taking part.

Consistent with our typical lab practice, data exclusion criteria were (1) Subjects who responded with the same key for more than 80% of trials (response bias), (2) Subjects with more than 20% of trials with reaction times <200 ms (fast responses) or >7,500 ms (slow responses), (3) Subjects with poor overall performance (difference between hits and false alarms < 0.05).

To ask whether the variability of memorability itself was reduced, we estimated the reliability-corrected variance of concept memorability on the 559 concepts tested in both sets: participants were split at random into two halves (200 splits), concept corrected recognition was computed from the pooled trials of each half, and the covariance of the two halves' values across concepts, to which trial-to-trial noise does not contribute, was averaged over splits.
Thus, we strongly believe future memorability studies should use a more standard study-test design or at minimum ensure participants are reliably above floor on false alarm rates.

The final sample was the first 100 participants, recruited online through Prolific, who passed the preregistered exclusion rule (at least 4 of the 6 repeats detected and no more than 5 presses to non-repeated faces during study); 11 additional participants were run and excluded under this rule.
We chose them to match our participants' overall false alarm rate and to come close to their overall hit rate.
Participants were told to memorize the images for a later memory test.
The final sample consisted of 50 participants recruited from UC San Diego who took part in this study in exchange for course credit.
Four additional participants were run and excluded based on the above criteria.Image Set Structure Experiments.

The final sample consisted of 450 participants across the three image sets: 150 participants in the maintained image set, 150 participants in the changed image set, and 150 participants in the reduced image set, all of whom were recruited from UC San Diego and took part in this study in exchange for course credit.

Across all 3 stimulus set experiments, 152 additional participants were excluded based on the above criteria.Experiments were run online and completed on participants' personal devices.Recognition Memory Task.
Within each of six higher-level categories, participants were split into quartiles by how many exemplars of that category they saw.

text.text: Some pictures, videos, faces, voices, videogame sprites and words are reliably remembered better than others, a phenomenon known as memorability.
This has been widely interpreted as reflecting a stable, intrinsic property of the stimuli.
Here we argue that this consistency is better explained by the relational structure of the stimulus sets used to measure memorability than by an intrinsic property of the items.

Using simulations with a global matching model of recognition memory, we show that apparent intrinsic memorability emerges naturally from distinctiveness (how dissimilar an item is from others in a set of encoded images and during the memory test) without any stimulus-intrinsic mechanism.

In targeted behavioral experiments, we demonstrate that manipulating the similarity structure of image sets can invert memorability rankings, making previously memorable images forgettable and vice versa.

We show that features previously identified as intrinsically memorable (e.g., "body-part related") are the most representationally distinctive features in standard image sets, explaining their memorability.

To address these large variations in distinctiveness we created a new image set that reduced variability in representational distinctiveness, and found that this significantly diminished the relationship between features and memorability.
These findings suggest that memorability need not reflect intrinsic properties of stimuli, but can emerge from their relational distinctiveness within a given context.

Because findings previously interpreted as evidence of intrinsic memorability are naturally accommodated by longstanding global matching models of recognition memory, the existence of an intrinsic memorability component, if any exists, remains to be demonstrated.
Some images are remembered better than others, and this has been widely taken to reflect a property of the images themselves.
We show that the same pattern emerges from how distinctive each image is within the stimulus set it was drawn from.
Thus, the choice of an image set, and of how to sample from it to choose study and test images, determines which images look memorable.

Researchers should treat the representational structure of their stimulus sets as part of the design, and ask how it shapes their conclusions before attributing stable psychological properties to the stimuli themselves.

Some pictures (Isola et al., 2014), videos (Cohendet et al., 2019), faces (Bainbridge et al., 2013), voices (Revsine et al., 2025), videogame sprites (Simpson et al., 2025), and words (Xie et al., 2020) are reliably remembered better than others, in a pattern that is strikingly consistent across people.

text.text: This consistency, referred to as memorability, has become one of the most actively studied phenomena in memory research over the past decade (Bainbridge et al., 2026; Rust & Mehrpour, 2020).
text.formatted: This consistency, referred to as memorability, has become one of the most actively studied phenomena in memory research over the past decade <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bainbridge et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rust & Mehrpour, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The prevailing theoretical view of this consistency between people in memory performance is that memorability is an intrinsic property of stimuli: some images simply are more memorable, much like some images are brighter or more colorful (Khosla et al., 2015; Needell & Bainbridge, 2022).
text.formatted: The prevailing theoretical view of this consistency between people in memory performance is that memorability is an intrinsic property of stimuli: some images simply are more memorable, much like some images are brighter or more colorful <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Khosla et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Needell & Bainbridge, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This intrinsic interpretation of memorability has drawn support from several converging lines of evidence.
Memorability rankings remain stable across different experimental contexts and participant populations (Bylinskii et al., 2015; Kramer et al., 2023; Revsine & Bainbridge, 2025).
text.formatted: Memorability rankings remain stable across different experimental contexts and participant populations <ref type="bibr">(Bylinskii et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Revsine & Bainbridge, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Memorability can be predicted from patterns of activation in the visual cortex to single images shown in isolation (Bainbridge et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Memorability can be predicted from patterns of activation in the visual cortex to single images shown in isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bainbridge et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: And deep learning models like MemNet (Khosla et al., 2015) and ResMem (Needell & Bainbridge, 2022), which take only a single image as input and have no information about the observer or the experimental context, can predict average memory performance with considerable accuracy.
text.formatted: And deep learning models like MemNet <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Khosla et al., 2015)</ref> and ResMem <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Needell & Bainbridge, 2022)</ref>, which take only a single image as input and have no information about the observer or the experimental context, can predict average memory performance with considerable accuracy.

text.text: Memorability researchers have argued that memorability is intrinsic because it reflects something fundamental about how efficiently individual images are processed visually (e.g., Bainbridge et al., 2026) or about the informational utility those particular images hold for the observer.
text.formatted: Memorability researchers have argued that memorability is intrinsic because it reflects something fundamental about how efficiently individual images are processed visually (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bainbridge et al., 2026)</ref> or about the informational utility those particular images hold for the observer.

text.text: For example, animate stimuli, social stimuli, and emotional stimuli are simultaneously more relevant to ongoing decisions on average and also more memorable (Boger & Firestone, 2026; Bylinskii et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, animate stimuli, social stimuli, and emotional stimuli are simultaneously more relevant to ongoing decisions on average and also more memorable <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boger & Firestone, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bylinskii et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In the current paper, we propose an alternative.

We argue that memorability is not intrinsic to an image but is an emergent property of how the structure of the stimulus sets used in memorability experiments shapes the context in which each item is studied and tested.

This alternative starts from a simple observation: nearly every formal model of recognition memory developed over the past fifty years treats memory as fundamentally relational, rather than memory signals being intrinsic to a given stimulus (Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984; Hintzman, 1988; McClelland & Chappell, 1998; Nosofsky, 1988; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: This alternative starts from a simple observation: nearly every formal model of recognition memory developed over the past fifty years treats memory as fundamentally relational, rather than memory signals being intrinsic to a given stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gillund & Shiffrin, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hintzman, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">McClelland & Chappell, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nosofsky, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: This class of models, termed global matching models, is the dominant theoretical framework for recognition because these models account for a wide range of core phenomena within a unified architecture (Osth & Dennis, 2024).
text.formatted: This class of models, termed global matching models, is the dominant theoretical framework for recognition because these models account for a wide range of core phenomena within a unified architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Osth & Dennis, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In global matching models, whether a person judges an item as "old" or "new" depends not on any fixed property of that item but on how that item relates to everything else in memory and to the 'lures' (new items) shown at test.

The match signal generated by a test item reflects its overall match to all stored memory traces, not just the single best match (if you have seen many images of mugs, all mugs will feel familiar at test).

The criterion for responding "old" based on that signal is then calibrated to the expected distribution of match signals (if you studied all items briefly, you will accept even weak signals as evidence of oldness) and to the evidence provided by each match (often based on the rarity of a feature).

These two kinds of relational processing (relative to the list and relative to the test) create a strong dependence of memory on distinctiveness, such that items that are unusual relative to other encoded items and test lures generate more diagnostic signals and are better discriminated as in memory or not (Hunt, 1995; Konkle et al., 2010; Nairne, 2006; Schmidt, 1991).
text.formatted: These two kinds of relational processing (relative to the list and relative to the test) create a strong dependence of memory on distinctiveness, such that items that are unusual relative to other encoded items and test lures generate more diagnostic signals and are better discriminated as in memory or not <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hunt, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Konkle et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Nairne, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schmidt, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: The advantage of distinctive items is one of the oldest and most robust findings in the memory literature, particularly in recall (Hunt & Lamb, 2001; von Restorff, 1933; for a review, see MacLeod, 2020).
text.formatted: The advantage of distinctive items is one of the oldest and most robust findings in the memory literature, particularly in recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hunt & Lamb, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">von Restorff, 1933</ref>; for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">MacLeod, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Memorability researchers acknowledge that local context influences memory measurements, and therefore have frequently attempted to distinguish between extrinsic memorability factors (like attentional states or individual differences) and intrinsic stimulus factors that are claimed to explain unique variance in memory performance (e.g., Bainbridge, 2020; Bylinskii et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Memorability researchers acknowledge that local context influences memory measurements, and therefore have frequently attempted to distinguish between extrinsic memorability factors (like attentional states or individual differences) and intrinsic stimulus factors that are claimed to explain unique variance in memory performance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bainbridge, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bylinskii et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In an attempt to isolate the intrinsic factors, experiments aimed at studying memorability have typically made the studied and tested items a particular participant sees be a random sample from large image sets like SUN (Xiao et al., 2016) or THINGS (Hebart et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In an attempt to isolate the intrinsic factors, experiments aimed at studying memorability have typically made the studied and tested items a particular participant sees be a random sample from large image sets like SUN <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Xiao et al., 2016)</ref> or THINGS <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These studies acknowledge contextual effects within any given list sampled from the image set but treat them as noise, on the assumption that randomly sampling images from a large image set should effectively randomize contextual effects, with any effects remaining across these randomized contexts reflecting properties intrinsic to the stimuli that will persist regardless of context.

In the current work, we show this does not isolate intrinsic memorability, both because memory is inherently relational and because the large-scale image sets from which memorability experiments draw their stimuli are not uniform samples of the space of images, nor proportional to how much representational space people have for these images.
They contain many more exemplars of some kinds of objects than others.

Items that happen to be distinctive within such an image set will tend to remain distinctive in any random subsample drawn from it, for the same reason that randomly sampling from a population does not eliminate confounds that are structural properties of that population (e.g., in the social sciences literature : Rothman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Items that happen to be distinctive within such an image set will tend to remain distinctive in any random subsample drawn from it, for the same reason that randomly sampling from a population does not eliminate confounds that are structural properties of that population (e.g., in the social sciences literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">: Rothman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, if an image occupies a sparse region of representational space within the image set, it will tend to be distinctive in every experiment that draws stimuli from that image set, and global matching models predict it will be reliably well discriminated from new items not because it possesses an intrinsic mnemonic property but because of its distinctiveness with respect to that image set and to the lures drawn from that image set.
By analogy, consider that red items are generally more visually salient than brown items in most visual environments.
Does this make red "intrinsically salient"?

Visual saliency models strongly reject this, and evidence has repeatedly shown that saliency is entirely relational, determined by how an item stands out relative to its local context (e.g., Itti & Koch, 2001).
text.formatted: Visual saliency models strongly reject this, and evidence has repeatedly shown that saliency is entirely relational, determined by how an item stands out relative to its local context (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Itti & Koch, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Red appears salient in many scenes not because that pattern of photoreceptor activation has intrinsic saliency, but because of the distributional regularities of red often being locally distinctive in natural environments.
In a scene where the grass and sky were red, a brown object would be more salient than a red one.
In a scene where everyone wears red, a brown jacket would stand out.

Similarly, we argue that what appears as intrinsic memorability may simply reflect how distinctive items are in a given large-scale image set rather than any fundamental property of the stimuli themselves.

In this paper, therefore, we test whether the evidence for intrinsic memorability can be better explained as emergent memorability: consistency across people that arises from the average distinctiveness of items in the average tested context.

Using simulations with wellestablished global matching models of recognition memory (REM; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; a hybrid-similarity exemplar model, Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), we first show that purely relational memory processes reproduce the key empirical signatures of intrinsic memorability (including consistency across different contexts) in models that have no concept of intrinsic stimulus properties being differentially memorable.
text.formatted: Using simulations with wellestablished global matching models of recognition memory (REM; <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997</ref>; a hybrid-similarity exemplar model, <ref type="bibr">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>, we first show that purely relational memory processes reproduce the key empirical signatures of intrinsic memorability (including consistency across different contexts) in models that have no concept of intrinsic stimulus properties being differentially memorable.

text.text: We then show in two experiments that memory is relational in exactly this way, such that changing what an item is studied with can invert memorability rankings, as can changing the features present in the lures at test.

Finally, we show that the features identified as "intrinsically memorable" in prior work are those that happen to be the most distinctive in the image sets used to measure them, and that changing or evening out the structure of an image set changes which features predict memorability.

These findings suggest that what has been characterized as a stable property of images is better understood as an emergent property of how images are situated within the broader representational structure of the contexts in which they are encountered and tested.

To highlight how global matching models can produce memorability effects, we conducted simulations using the REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory) model framework (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), which represents items as arbitrary vectors of feature values drawn from a geometric distribution, such that some feature values are more common than others.
text.formatted: To highlight how global matching models can produce memorability effects, we conducted simulations using the REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory) model framework <ref type="bibr">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, which represents items as arbitrary vectors of feature values drawn from a geometric distribution, such that some feature values are more common than others.

text.text: This model has been widely applied and found to explain core phenomena in recognition memory (Malmberg et al., 2019; Mohamed et al., 2026).

text.text: However, while numerous global matching models share the foundational principle that summed similarity (the aggregated similarity between a probe item and all stored memory traces) plays a central role in recognition decisions (e.g., Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Nosofsky, 1988; Osth & Dennis, 2024), we focus on REM because it implements this principle through an elegant Bayesian likelihood ratio framework, making it ideal for examining how apparent memorability effects emerge from relational distinctiveness.

text.text: Our core results also hold in other global matching models that give rare features extra weight, like a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003; see SI Appendix, Section 3).
text.formatted: Our core results also hold in other global matching models that give rare features extra weight, like a hybrid-similarity exemplar model <ref type="bibr">(Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003</ref>; see SI Appendix, Section 3).

text.text: In particular, in judging whether an item is "old" or "new", REM uses what amounts to counterfactual Bayesian reasoning: it computes the likelihood that an observed memory match signal would occur if the item had been studied versus if it had not.
Consider a person with a distinctive face tattoo.

When a tattooed face is studied, the same face on a later recognition test may produce an exceptionally strong memory match signal not because it matches its memory representation better than an average face without a tattoo would, but because the tattoo is rare and therefore greatly reduces the probability of a similar match signal arising from a face that was not studied.

In terms of the likelihood ratio, the rare feature primarily affects the denominator, since the probability of such a match under the alternative hypothesis that the face was not studied is very small.
Therefore, when a match occurs along this rare dimension, it constitutes exceptionally strong evidence that this particular person was studied.
However, this is not intrinsic memorability, because it is always a ratio that depends fundamentally on the lures, not just the shown item.
Thus, any other face with the same kind of tattoo will also generate strong 'old' evidence and thus many false alarms, as we find in our face experiment below.

In contrast, an average person without distinctive features may actually be more similar to other studied faces (e.g., have a higher summed similarity to the memory set), yet produce a weaker recognition signal because many unstudied faces also share these common features, making them not very diagnostic of a true match.

We generated simulated data that had the same approximate structure as the most well understood memorability dataset (Kramer et al., 2023), which provides memorability scores for the images and features of the THINGS image set (Hebart et al., 2019). Hebart et al. (2020) showed that human similarity judgments for this image set were well captured by a sparse set of 49 distinct visual/semantic features.

(2020)</ref> showed that human similarity judgments for this image set were well captured by a sparse set of 49 distinct visual/semantic features.

text.text: We therefore generated a set of 1,600 simulated items (the size of the image sets in our behavioral experiments), each represented by a vector of 49 feature values to match these human data in approximate structure.

In our simulation, the 49 feature values for each item were generated randomly and independently from a geometric distribution (see Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), and thus have no particular meaning and no intrinsic relationship to memorability.
text.formatted: In our simulation, the 49 feature values for each item were generated randomly and independently from a geometric distribution (see <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, and thus have no particular meaning and no intrinsic relationship to memorability.

text.text: Items were then "shown" to the model, and episodic memory encoding followed the standard REM procedure (SI Appendix, Section 1).
To mimic the structure of typical memorability experiments as well as our subsequent behavioral experiments, we designed the study and test items to be random subsets of this simulated image set.

In particular, mimicking our behavioral experiments, we conducted 10,000 independent recognition memory experiment simulations, each involving a simulated participant studying a random draw of 40 items and then being tested on 40 items: 20 of the studied items (old) intermixed with 20 additional items drawn from the 1,600-item set that were not studied in that simulation (new lures).

For each simulated recognition test, we compute the hit rate (calling an item old when it was old) for each item and the false alarm rate (calling an item old when it was new) for that same item across the 10,000 simulation runs.
Accurate measures of memorability would require ROC analysis (e.g., Brady et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Accurate measures of memorability would require ROC analysis (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Brady et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, for comparison to the existing memorability literature, we focus here on hit rate and/or corrected recognition rate (hits minus false alarms).
All of our analyses are robust to using d′ or d a (SI Appendix, Sections 1 and 2).
We find that some items are consistently more memorable than others across "participants" (Fig. 1a), mimicking apparent intrinsic memorability.
text.formatted: We find that some items are consistently more memorable than others across "participants" (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>), mimicking apparent intrinsic memorability.

text.text: However, in this simulation all features are randomly generated and contain no actual semantic or visual information that could make them intrinsically memorable.

Thus, this memorability could not be predicted by anything intrinsic about the features themselves, but instead was strongly predicted by each item's distinctiveness in the overall image set (i.e., how dissimilar it was to other items in the image set).
As noted above, many specific aspects of the distinctiveness of an item and its features play a role in REM's decision via the likelihood ratio.

However, in line with the general structure of global matching models, we found items that are more similar to other items in aggregate (summed similarity of raw feature representations, not differentiating by rare vs. common features as REM does) have greater interference in matching and thus worse memory performance (memorability vs. summed similarity to all other items across all of the features: r = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.52], p < 0.01; Fig. 1a).
text.formatted: However, in line with the general structure of global matching models, we found items that are more similar to other items in aggregate (summed similarity of raw feature representations, not differentiating by rare vs. common features as REM does) have greater interference in matching and thus worse memory performance (memorability vs. summed similarity to all other items across all of the features: r = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.52], p < 0.01; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: As described in the supplement, the breakdown of this effect into hits vs. false alarms depends on the nature of the crowding in the stimulus set and the way the model weights rarity vs. summed similarity (SI Appendix, Section 4).

A core conclusion of the memorability literature has been that not only do images vary in memorability, but this image-level variance is predictable based on the features of the images (Kramer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: A core conclusion of the memorability literature has been that not only do images vary in memorability, but this image-level variance is predictable based on the features of the images <ref type="bibr">(Kramer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For example, of the 49 visual and semantic features, some predict better memorability (e.g., body part-relatedness) and some worse memorability (e.g., electronics).
Does the same occur here, where features are arbitrary and such relationships could not be intrinsic?
In our simulations, individual features also show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: In our simulations, individual features also show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: Crucially, however, each feature's correlation with memorability was predicted by how much that feature correlated with overall item similarity, not by anything intrinsic to the features (as nothing could be intrinsic here, with arbitrary features: ρ = -0.44, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.30], p < 0.01; Fig. 1b).

text.text: Overall, with no intrinsic features that are in any way tied to memorability, REM reproduces the key aspects of the data that are generally argued to provide evidence for intrinsic memorability.

This is evidence that such a pattern is not diagnostic of intrinsic memorability, but can arise from the distribution of studied items and lures in an arbitrary stimulus set with a fully relational model, where rarity weights feature matches and summed similarity drives decisions in the same way to both old and new items.

REM also reproduces what has been offered as the strongest evidence for intrinsic memorability, that the rank order of items' memorability is stable across large changes in context (Bylinskii et al., 2015).
text.formatted: REM also reproduces what has been offered as the strongest evidence for intrinsic memorability, that the rank order of items' memorability is stable across large changes in context <ref type="bibr">(Bylinskii et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In a simulation of Bylinskii et al.'s within-category and across-category contexts, items kept their memorability ranks across contexts (Spearman ρ = 0.60, 95% CI [0.56, 0.63]; ρ = 0.60 for hit rates in the human data), because adding many items from the same category raised the summed similarity of every item in that category without actually changing which of them were the most distinctive (ρ = 0.93, 95% CI [0.92, 0.94]; SI Appendix, Section 3).
Importantly, these results (and this cross-context consistency) do not appear to depend on the particular settings we chose for the simulations.

They held across a wide range of REM's parameters and decision criteria, in continuous recognition as well as study-test lists, and when the simulated items were given the measured features of THINGS concepts rather than randomly generated ones as well as in a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Nosofsky et al., 2025; SI Appendix, Section 3).

text.text: Because global matching models have been a dominant theoretical framework in recognition memory for decades, supported by a large body of empirical evidence, we suggest that the burden of proof shifts to the intrinsic memorability account: what positive evidence supports it?

While we cannot prove intrinsic memorability does not exist, we can test a set of predictions that is unique to global matching models, namely that explicitly manipulating similarity structure should change what appears memorable and that memorability in existing image sets should follow the similarity structure of the items studied and tested.

Our first behavioral experiment directly tests whether the predictions of global matching models generalize from simulations to human memory by attempting to invert memorability rankings through systematic manipulation of study context, with test context held fixed.

Notably, we manipulate context in a way that does not just shift all items upward and downward in terms of their overall similarity to other items studied (as in Bylinskii et al., 2015, which is not diagnostic of emergent vs. intrinsic memorability, as shown by the simulation), but instead differentially shifts distinctiveness across items.
text.formatted: Notably, we manipulate context in a way that does not just shift all items upward and downward in terms of their overall similarity to other items studied (as in <ref type="bibr">Bylinskii et al., 2015, which</ref> is not diagnostic of emergent vs. intrinsic memorability, as shown by the simulation), but instead differentially shifts distinctiveness across items.

text.text: In each study/test block, we selected five critical items from the THINGS image set spanning the full memorability range based on Kramer et al.'s (2023) scores, one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins.
text.formatted: In each study/test block, we selected five critical items from the THINGS image set spanning the full memorability range based on <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al.'s (2023)</ref> scores, one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins.

text.text: We then constructed the similarity context around each critical item.

Originally highly memorable items were surrounded in the study list by many similar items from the image set (8 similar items, with 4, 2 and 1 for the intermediate bins; SI Appendix, Section 1), reducing their distinctiveness in the list context.
Conversely, originally poorly memorable items were placed in lists with few or no similar items (0 similar items), making them the most distinctive items in their list context.
This approach directly manipulates the relational property of distinctiveness while keeping the intrinsic properties of the items themselves unchanged.

Consistent with our emergent account, when comparing the original memorability scores of the items from Kramer et al. (2023) against the memorability in this task, we found a significant inversion (ρ = -0.50, 95% CI [-0.76, -0.18], p < 0.01; see Fig. 1c).
text.formatted: Consistent with our emergent account, when comparing the original memorability scores of the items from <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al. (2023)</ref> against the memorability in this task, we found a significant inversion (ρ = -0.50, 95% CI [-0.76, -0.18], p < 0.01; see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>).

text.text: This suggests that the distinctiveness was a better predictor of item memorability than intrinsic properties of the images.
The inversion experiment changed what each item was studied alongside without changing the test structure.
However, global matching models also predict that what an item is tested against should be key to its memorability.
Our second experiment tests this prediction with faces, focusing on a version of the tattoo example above.
In particular, we held the studied faces fixed and changed only whether a new face at test contained the same rare feature.
Participants studied 50 faces (N = 100, preregistered; SI Appendix, Section 5).
Six of the 50 studied faces had a feature that is rare in everyday life (e.g., an electricgreen mohawk).
Each rare feature was present on two different people.
One of them was studied, and the other could sometimes appear at test as a lure with the same rare feature.
The rest of the test was ordinary faces, half of them studied and half new.
If a rare feature makes a face intrinsically memorable, a studied rare face should be easy to tell apart from any new face.
If memorability is relational, the rare feature should help only when no new face at test also has it.
Studied faces with a rare feature were called old on 90% of trials, compared with 80% for ordinary studied faces (t(99) = 5.29, p < 0.001).
text.formatted: Studied faces with a rare feature were called old on 90% of trials, compared with 80% for ordinary studied faces (t(99) = 5.29, p < 0.001).

text.text: Unrelated new faces, which had no rare feature, were called old on only 41% of trials.
Against these new faces, rare faces were much more discriminable than ordinary faces (d a = 1.67 vs.
1.00; Fig. 1d, red line).

text.text: However, the new face with the same rare feature was called old on 59% of trials (0.18 more often than an unrelated new face, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001).
text.formatted: However, the new face with the same rare feature was called old on 59% of trials (0.18 more often than an unrelated new face, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001).

text.text: The rare feature thus raised false alarms even more than it raised hits (by 0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033).
Against this lure, the same rare faces were no more discriminable than an ordinary face (d a = 1.00, 95% CI [0.75, 1.25]; Fig. 1d, blue dashed line).
text.formatted: Against this lure, the same rare faces were no more discriminable than an ordinary face (d a = 1.00, 95% CI [0.75, 1.25]; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1d</ref>, blue dashed line).

text.text: Comparing each face against itself across participants, the rare faces were also no more memorable than ordinary faces (hit rate minus false alarm rate 0.33 vs.
0.38), because their extra hits were matched by extra false alarms (SI Appendix, Section 5).
Thus, a rare feature of the kind usually thought to make a face memorable did not make that face intrinsically more memorable.
Matching on the rare feature was strong evidence that a face was studied, whether or not the rest of the face matched, rather than providing any facespecific advantage.
Overall, both of our targeted experiments changed the context an item was judged in while holding the item itself constant.
The first changed how many similar items were studied alongside the item, and the second whether a similar item appeared at test.
If memorability were intrinsic, neither manipulation should matter, since the images and the faces were the same in every condition.
Global matching models predict both effects we observed, in particular a cost to similarity in both situations in terms of the ability to discriminate old from new items.
Thus, we suggest, in line with decades of work on recognition memory, that a memorability score is necessarily a claim about both an item and the set it was measured in.
We next turn to memorability in large-scale image sets, the primary domain that has been the focus of the intrinsic memorability literature.

To understand real-world memorability in this context, where similarity is not explicitly manipulated (or simulated), we must specify the representational space within which distinctiveness operates in human memory.
Before any particular memory episode occurs, perception and cognition have already structured the world into a particular representational format.

Episodic memory operates on top of this pre-existing structure, such that when we encode a particular image or event, the memory representation inherits the structure and biases of the underlying perceptual and semantic space (e.g., Nagy et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Episodic memory operates on top of this pre-existing structure, such that when we encode a particular image or event, the memory representation inherits the structure and biases of the underlying perceptual and semantic space (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Nagy et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a key question for understanding human memorability in real image sets: what are the "features" that determine distinctiveness in human cognition?
Clearly people represent some aspects of the environment more than others (e.g., faces more than blades of grass), and this will shape their representations and thus memory confusions.
This shaping is evident in the representational space of the THINGS image set (the dominant image set used to study memorability).

The similarity structure of this image set, as captured by the 49dimensional feature embedding that explains human similarity judgments (Hebart et al., 2020), devotes substantial representational capacity to features related to animacy (body parts, animals, insects) because human cognition allocates disproportionate neural and attentional resources to animate things, given their ecological and social importance (Nairne et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The similarity structure of this image set, as captured by the 49dimensional feature embedding that explains human similarity judgments <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020)</ref>, devotes substantial representational capacity to features related to animacy (body parts, animals, insects) because human cognition allocates disproportionate neural and attentional resources to animate things, given their ecological and social importance <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Nairne et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: How will this impact memory?
Consider the 49-dimensional THINGS representational space.

If an image set contains many animate items, such that animate items are common on individual study lists and as test lures, they will occupy densely packed regions of representational space, making individual animate items less distinctive and therefore less memorable.
Conversely, if animate items are rare in an image set and therefore rare on individual study lists and test sets, they become highly distinctive within that context.

Thus, the apparent "intrinsic memorability" of animate items in standard image sets need not reflect animacy itself, nor the extra representational capacity devoted to those features, but the fact that animate items are relatively sparse in the image set despite falling in a region of representational space to which humans devote substantial resources.

Although humans clearly represent more and richer features about some stimuli than others, this does not allow one to make any prediction about memorability per se without also taking into account the over-or underrepresentation of items in the image set, and thus the study and test sets, relative to this representational space.

To test the emergent memorability account, we used the THINGS image set to construct three complementary representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs), operationalizing how similar vs. dissimilar items were in this representational space in order to allow us to examine the degree of over-vs. underrepresentation and what it predicts about memory performance.
One similarity structure was derived from the 49-dimensional feature embeddings known to capture human similarity judgments (Hebart et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One similarity structure was derived from the 49-dimensional feature embeddings known to capture human similarity judgments <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A second was based on macaque IT cortex neural activity patterns (Papale et al., 2025), serving as a biological model of object representation.
text.formatted: A second was based on macaque IT cortex neural activity patterns <ref type="bibr">(Papale et al., 2025)</ref>, serving as a biological model of object representation.

text.text: Both these 49-dimensional features and IT patterns are at the concept/category level, not the image level.

Thus, where required to get individual image predictions, we also use a third similarity structure, an RDM based on pooled computer vision models (ResNet18, VGG16, AlexNet, and CLIP), though given this is unlikely to be well aligned with humans (see Simpson et al., 2026) we use human and monkey data where possible.

text.text: Note that these

As noted, the targeted inversion and face experiments differ from conventional memorability paradigms in a crucial way, in that we deliberately constructed the similarity context, at study in the first and at test in the second, rather than randomly sampling from a large image set.
We did this in order to show directly that memory performance depends crucially on both of these factors and cannot be understood without considering which other items are present at study and test.
Standard memorability studies instead sample items at random from large image sets, in order to average over many similarity contexts (e.g., Isola et al., 2014; Kramer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Standard memorability studies instead sample items at random from large image sets, in order to average over many similarity contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Isola et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: If our distinctiveness account is correct, however, then random sampling cannot eliminate these effects.

Instead, the similarity structure of the image set itself should determine which items appear memorable, even when items are randomly sampled for individual experiments, because sampling from the image sets determines the average context at study and test.

Study context is straightforward to see, but test context is also likely critical to why image sets affect memorability (e.g., in THINGS, an image of a face is, on average, much less similar to the lures it is tested against than an image of a chainsaw is).

This is the dependence on lures that we isolated in our face experiment (Fig. 1d), except that in a standard memorability study the image set, rather than the experimenter, decides how often the lures share an item's features.
text.formatted: This is the dependence on lures that we isolated in our face experiment (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1d</ref>), except that in a standard memorability study the image set, rather than the experimenter, decides how often the lures share an item's features.

text.text: By measuring distinctiveness in similarity spaces derived from human judgments and from neural data, we next assess whether putatively intrinsically memorable items stand out from their context along dimensions that are psychologically and biologically meaningful in previous memorability data, as global matching models predict.
To test this, we reanalyzed the Kramer et al. (2023) memorability findings, asking how the structure of the image set predicts which 'features' predict item memorability.
text.formatted: To test this, we reanalyzed the <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al. (2023)</ref> memorability findings, asking how the structure of the image set predicts which 'features' predict item memorability.

text.text: We focus on Kramer et al. (2023) because their work provides in many ways the strongest and most interpretable evidence for the intrinsic memorability account.
text.formatted: We focus on <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al. (2023)</ref> because their work provides in many ways the strongest and most interpretable evidence for the intrinsic memorability account.

text.text: They show how the 49 features derived from human similarity data in the THINGS image set (Hebart et al., 2020) relate to memorability.
text.formatted: They show how the 49 features derived from human similarity data in the THINGS image set <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020</ref>) relate to memorability.

text.text: They find, for example, that images high on the body-part related feature are among the best remembered by participants, whereas items that score high on the electronics/technology feature tend to be poorly remembered by participants.

This feature-level analysis offers both greater statistical power and greater interpretability than item-level memorability scores alone: rather than asking whether a particular image happens to be well-remembered with no clear explanation for why, they ask which psychological dimensions systematically predict memorability.
We can therefore straightforwardly ask whether those dimensions are also ones that track distinctiveness within the structure of the image set.
The feature-based analysis is also likely to be more straightforward at the concept level than at the image level.

Any noise in the representations we assume for items, or systematic deviations in these representations from actual human representations, will necessarily reduce the ability of a distinctiveness-based account to explain real memorability data (Simpson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Any noise in the representations we assume for items, or systematic deviations in these representations from actual human representations, will necessarily reduce the ability of a distinctiveness-based account to explain real memorability data <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Simpson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, the greater reliability of measures at the feature level provides a stronger test of how much can be explained by distinctiveness, alleviating this concern to a significant extent.
In agreement with Kramer et al., we find that individual features out of the 49 visual and semantic features isolated by Hebart et al. (2020) show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. 2a).
text.formatted: In agreement with Kramer et al., we find that individual features out of the 49 visual and semantic features isolated by <ref type="bibr">Hebart et al. (2020)</ref> show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref>).

text.text: However, we also find that the features most predictive of memorability are those that, in the THINGS image set, are most related to distinctiveness, as the emergent memorability view strongly predicts and the intrinsic memorability view gives no reason to expect.

In particular, the extent to which features predict memorability is strongly related to the extent to which those features predict overcrowding in the image set (summed similarity vs. memorability: r = -0.612, 95% CI [-0.677, -0.505], p < 0.001; Fig. 2a).

text.text: Measured with d′, the relationship holds whether crowding is computed over the nearest concepts or over the whole image set, and crowded concepts draw more false alarms at every scale (SI Appendix, Section 4).

Similarly, using activity along the monkey multi-unit array as our features (see SI Appendix, Section 1 for further details), we find that features that predict human memorability also predict summed similarity in the neural representations (r = -0.296, 95% CI [-0.389, -0.176], p < 0.001), although naturally these measures are less reliable and less aligned with human representations.

text.text: In other words, "body-part related" predicts memorability, as Kramer et al. showed.

However, it is also one of the best predictors of low summed similarity to other items in the THINGS image set, making such items on average unique at study and at test, a highly diagnostic prediction unique to emergent memorability theories that intrinsic accounts have no reason to expect.
This relationship does not appear to be specific to the published embedding or to object images.

Summed similarity computed from the features of deep networks also predicts memorability in the most well studied dataset of face memorability (Bainbridge et al., 2013) and a core dataset on scene memorability (Isola et al., 2011), with this summed similarity measure predicting about two thirds of the maximum possible correlation with memorability in these datasets despite the intrinsic memorability account having no reason to expect any relationship to summed similarity at all (SI Appendix, Section 6).

text.text: While this continuous recognition paradigm does not allow careful isolation of study and test, or computation of more accurate memory measures (SI Appendix, Section 2), we nonetheless find that the same image was remembered less well when the images that preceded it in a participant's stream were more similar to it, regardless of whether similarity was measured from human judgments or in a purely visual space derived from deep networks (SI Appendix, Section 7).

When we ranked each image's trials by how similar the preceding stream was, d′ fell by 0.51 (95% CI [0.48, 0.54]) from the least to the most similar context, 1.34 times the standard deviation of d′ across images (SI Appendix, Fig. S15a).

text.text: When we ran Kramer et al.'s own test for context (which they argued contributed minimally) on the same trials, it left the image rankings intact, because as in our REM simulations, splitting participants by how many exemplars of a category they saw shifts the competitors of every image in that category at once (SI Appendix, Fig. S16) and thus masks the role of context.

text.text: Thus, the mismatch between how densely THINGS samples a region of representational space and how much of that space people devote to it (e.g., few animate concepts but many electronics) leads features like body parts to appear intrinsically memorable when they may owe their memorability to being underrepresented in the image set relative to the richness with which humans process and represent them.
We next consider a key causal prediction of the emergent memorability account with respect to this image set argument.

If we systematically change the similarity structure of an image set, features that were originally "intrinsically memorable" should lose their memorability advantage, while a new set of features should emerge as apparently memorable.

This prediction directly contradicts purely intrinsic views of memorability, which predict that features maintain their memorability regardless of the makeup of the image set that is used to test memorability.

To directly test whether memorability is a consequence of similarity structure rather than an intrinsic property of images, we subsampled the THINGS image set into two image sets of 1,600 images each, with contrasting representational distributions (Fig. 2b and c).
text.formatted: To directly test whether memorability is a consequence of similarity structure rather than an intrinsic property of images, we subsampled the THINGS image set into two image sets of 1,600 images each, with contrasting representational distributions (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2b</ref> and <ref type="figure">c</ref>).

text.text: Throughout, the similarity space is fixed, insofar as each concept has the same coordinates in the 49dimensional embedding in both image sets and in every model and analysis.
The sets differ only in which concepts are sampled, and therefore in how crowded each concept's neighborhood is at study and test.
The first (the maintained image set) preserved the original similarity structure of the full image set.

The second (the changed image set) sampled the same space differently, partially inverting which regions were crowded (to the degree possible), so that concepts previously occupying crowded and overrepresented regions of feature space now became relatively distinct.
It was not possible to fully invert the similarity structure because of the discrete nature of the image set, e.g., only so many animate items were available when subsampling the THINGS image set.

Nonetheless, the changed image set switched the relative prevalence of different features in the image set, and thus changed the similarity structure with respect to the Hebart et al. (2020) features.

Because the lures were drawn from the same image set as the study lists, this also changed which features were distinctive relative to the lures (e.g., the changed set oversampled concepts high on features that had predicted good memory in THINGS, so that these concepts now met many close competitors at test).
If memorability were intrinsic to images, the same features should predict memory performance regardless of which image set a given image appears in.
Instead, in a recognition memory experiment with these stimuli (SI Appendix, Section 1), we found the opposite.

The relationships between features and memorability in the maintained image set closely replicated those of the full THINGS image set (r = 0.84, 95% CI [0.79, 0.86], p < 0.001; Fig. 2d), and distinctiveness in this image set predicted memorability, using both human and monkey similarity spaces to measure distinctiveness (r = -0.89, 95% CI [-0.91, -0.85], and r = -0.63, 95% CI [-0.68, -0.53], respectively; both p < 0.001).

text.text: When similarity structure was changed, however, the same features that had previously predicted good memory now predicted poor memory (r = -0.33, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.21], p < 0.001), with a new set of features becoming memorable.

text.text: The particular features that were now memorable were again predicted by their distinctiveness in both human (r = -0.75, 95% CI [-0.81, -0.64], p < 0.001) and monkey (r = -0.45, 95% CI [-0.51, -0.36], p < 0.001) similarity spaces, even though they were different features compared to the maintained image set.

text.text: These results show that which features are memorable is not fixed but depends on the context in which images are encountered, which is determined by the image set that lists are sampled from.

In addition, when we gave a global matching model the same study lists and test trials that our participants saw, it reproduced the inversion of Fig. 1c and correctly predicted that an image would be better remembered in the image set where it was more distinctive (SI Appendix, Section 8).
text.formatted: In addition, when we gave a global matching model the same study lists and test trials that our participants saw, it reproduced the inversion of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref> and correctly predicted that an image would be better remembered in the image set where it was more distinctive (SI Appendix, Section 8).

text.text: The observed change in memory for the same image between sets came mostly from false alarms, that is, from how often participants called the image old when it was a lure (SI Appendix, Section 8).
The relationship between summed similarity and memorability, at the level of both concepts and features, also did not depend on our participant exclusion criteria (SI Appendix, Section 1).

Some proponents of intrinsic memorability acknowledge that extrinsic effects (like overloading with similar items, as in the changed image set) may impact memorability in addition to intrinsic effects (e.g., Bylinskii et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Some proponents of intrinsic memorability acknowledge that extrinsic effects (like overloading with similar items, as in the changed image set) may impact memorability in addition to intrinsic effects (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Bylinskii et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In theory, then, intrinsic memorability could still exist, with all of our reported effects being extrinsic memorability effects that ride on top of these intrinsic effects.

Notably, there is no positive evidence for this, as we have shown so far that the full set of results typically taken to reflect intrinsic memorability can easily arise in simpler models that have no such concept, and tested direct causal predictions of our emergent account.

However, we reasoned that if memorability variation arises largely from distinctiveness variation, then sampling as uniformly from representational space as possible should reduce variability in distinctiveness and diminish the variability typically observed in how different features relate to memorability, without any overloading of similar items (in the resulting image set, no category made up more than about 13% of the concepts).

Because the lures are drawn from the same image set, such sampling should also reduce the variability in how distinctive features are, on average, relative to the lures, and so weaken how strongly any given feature predicts memorability.
By contrast, if memorability were intrinsic, visual features should predict memorability as strongly in such an image set as in the original and maintained image sets above.

In building this new image set, we were able to reduce summed similarity variation: whereas the maintained image set showed broad variability in summed similarity across concepts (Mean = 0.18, SD = 0.00322), reflecting the uneven crowding of representational space that characterizes the THINGS image set, the reduced variability image set showed a sharply peaked distribution around the same mean (SD = 0.00156), confirming that differences in distinctiveness had been successfully reduced (Fig. 2b and SI Appendix, Fig. S1).
text.formatted: In building this new image set, we were able to reduce summed similarity variation: whereas the maintained image set showed broad variability in summed similarity across concepts (Mean = 0.18, SD = 0.00322), reflecting the uneven crowding of representational space that characterizes the THINGS image set, the reduced variability image set showed a sharply peaked distribution around the same mean (SD = 0.00156), confirming that differences in distinctiveness had been successfully reduced (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2b</ref> and SI Appendix, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S1</ref>).

text.text: This almost certainly overstates how far we equalized true distinctiveness (e.g., we equated concepts rather than individual images, and the 49 features capture only some of the dimensions along which people confuse items), which will necessarily attenuate any reduction in the correlations between features and memorability.
Nonetheless, consistent with our emergent memorability account, this attempted equalization of distinctiveness substantially reduced the ability of image features to predict memorability.
Across all 49 features, the summed squared correlation with corrected recognition dropped by 27% relative to the maintained image set (one-sided bootstrap p = 0.036; Fig. 2h).
text.formatted: Across all 49 features, the summed squared correlation with corrected recognition dropped by 27% relative to the maintained image set (one-sided bootstrap p = 0.036; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2h</ref>).

text.text: Because the two image sets share only some of their concepts, we also repeated this analysis, as a more powerful test, on the 559 concepts that appear in both, holding the concepts and their features fixed.
On these concepts, the summed squared correlation dropped by 34% across 10,000 participant resamples (95% CI [4%, 57%], two-sided bootstrap p = 0.032).
Memorability also varied reliably less across concepts in the reduced set.

On the shared concepts, the reliability-corrected variance of concept memorability (the covariance of concept memorability between random halves of the participants, which trial-to-trial noise does not contribute to) was 38% lower in the reduced set (two-sided permutation p = 0.020, shuffling participants between the two sets).

Furthermore, the features that lost the most predictive power were those most tied to distinctiveness in the maintained set (Spearman ρ = 0.56 across the 49 features, p < 0.001; ρ = 0.37, p = 0.008, controlling for each feature's correlation with memorability in the maintained set).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the features that lost the most predictive power were those most tied to distinctiveness in the maintained set (Spearman ρ = 0.56 across the 49 features, p < 0.001; ρ = 0.37, p = 0.008, controlling for each feature's correlation with memorability in the maintained set).

text.text: This was true even though the reduced image set does not overload any one category and instead includes each category in study lists and as lures at test in a proportion closer to that implied by people's internal visual and semantic representation.
This pattern suggests that the closer an image set gets to being equally spaced in human representational space, the less image features predict memorability.
The present work challenges the view that some images are intrinsically more memorable than others.

Drawing on global matching models of recognition memory, we propose that what looks like intrinsic memorability is better understood as an emergent consequence of relational structure, that is, how similar or distinct an item is relative to everything else a person is tasked with remembering on a study list or discriminating it from at test.

We formalized this idea using global matching models, showing that distinctiveness within a stimulus set, not any fixed property of individual images, is sufficient to produce the memorability effects documented in the literature.
Directly manipulating context changed memorability in the way this account predicts.

When memorable images were surrounded by similar items at study, their memorability ranking inverted (ρ = -0.50), and a rare feature made a face more memorable only when no new face at test contained the same feature.

Reanalyses of the THINGS image set confirmed that the features that predict human memorability are precisely those that track distinctiveness within the image sets used to study memorability (r = -0.61).
Direct manipulations of image set structure showed that the same features can flip from memorable to forgettable depending on the image set images are sampled from.
Finally, reducing variation in how well features predict distinctiveness also reduced how well features predicted memorability (by 27%; Fig. 2h).
text.formatted: Finally, reducing variation in how well features predict distinctiveness also reduced how well features predicted memorability (by 27%; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2h</ref>).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that memorability is not a property to be explained at the level of individual images but a relational phenomenon that emerges from how distinct items are in visual and conceptual similarity.

Across these approaches, our results show that the methods used to establish intrinsic memorability (e.g., the consistency of memorability scores across participants within stimuli sampled randomly from the same image set or related image sets with the same biases) do not rule out a relational account, because any study that samples from the same image distribution will inherit the same similarity structure.

Thus, to establish that memorability is intrinsic rather than relational, one would need to show that images identified as memorable in one context retain that memorability advantage when placed in a context constructed to neutralize their distinctiveness.
Our experiments suggest they will not.
Other work has reached related conclusions from quite different directions.
For example, Nosofsky et al. (2025) show that a model based on relational similarity structure accounts for a wide range of context-dependent memorability effects in real-world image domains.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Nosofsky et al. (2025)</ref> show that a model based on relational similarity structure accounts for a wide range of context-dependent memorability effects in real-world image domains.

text.text: Their approach relies on fitting a cognitive model directly to individual-item recognition data rather than working at the level of image set structure.

Their model makes use of an item-level component (a self-similarity boost for items with salient distinctive features) that plays a role similar to the rare-feature weighting discussed below (see Distinctiveness Relative to the List and to Experience).

Similarly, Xie et al. (2020) modeled the memorability of words from their semantic similarity to other words (estimated from co-occurrence statistics), which is also a relational model of why some words are remembered better than others.

Other memorability work has addressed context directly, by sampling faces to represent a population or judging each face's distinctiveness on its own (Bainbridge et al., 2013) or by testing whether rankings survive changes in how many exemplars of a category participants saw (Kramer et al., 2023).

text.text: However, as noted in our reanalyses of these datasets, these tests ask whether a particular manipulation of list context drives a result rather than whether the structure of the sampled population or lists in general do.
In the same THINGS trials in which Kramer et al.'s test leaves rankings intact, we find that the same image is remembered less well after more similar items (SI Appendix, Section 7).

We suggest that the logic we apply to behavioral memorability also applies to the enthusiasm surrounding deep learning models of memorability, such as ResMem (Needell & Bainbridge, 2022) and its predecessor MemNet (Khosla et al., 2015).

text.text: It also applies to neural signatures of memorability identified in the brain, such as memorability-sensitive responses in the medial temporal lobe (Bainbridge et al., 2017) and the magnitude of the IT population response (Jaegle et al., 2019).
