text.text: The deep learning models achieve impressive prediction accuracy on their training distributions, and this success has been taken as evidence that memorability is a decodable intrinsic visual property.

Indeed, recent work has argued that because ResMem makes predictions from a single image with no access to the experimental context, its success demonstrates that it has identified properties intrinsic to the image (Davis & Bainbridge, 2023).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent work has argued that because ResMem makes predictions from a single image with no access to the experimental context, its success demonstrates that it has identified properties intrinsic to the image <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Davis & Bainbridge, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: But a model that learns to predict memorability scores from a fixed image distribution will necessarily internalize that distribution's similarity structure (just as language and vision models trained on human-generated data internalize their race and gender biases; Caliskan et al., 2017; Steed & Caliskan, 2021), and these models have no way to distinguish between an image that is memorable because of something fixed about it and an image that is memorable because it happens to be distinctive within the particular image set they were trained on.
text.formatted: But a model that learns to predict memorability scores from a fixed image distribution will necessarily internalize that distribution's similarity structure (just as language and vision models trained on human-generated data internalize their race and gender biases; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Caliskan et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Steed & Caliskan, 2021)</ref>, and these models have no way to distinguish between an image that is memorable because of something fixed about it and an image that is memorable because it happens to be distinctive within the particular image set they were trained on.

text.text: The lack of access to the experimental context at test time is therefore not the kind of independence from context needed to show that memorability is intrinsic.
The training distribution has already supplied the context of what the image is generally surrounded with at study and test.

Indeed, consistent with this view of internalized distinctiveness, Jaegle et al. (2019) found that the same correlation between response magnitude and memorability emerges in convolutional neural networks trained only to categorize objects, with no memory objective at all.
text.formatted: Indeed, consistent with this view of internalized distinctiveness, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jaegle et al. (2019)</ref> found that the same correlation between response magnitude and memorability emerges in convolutional neural networks trained only to categorize objects, with no memory objective at all.

text.text: We suggest the same holds for the brain.
A neural "marker" of memorability is, in our account, likely the average difference in response between kinds of stimuli that are under-vs. overrepresented in typical image sets.
Animacy, for example, is one of the largest dimensions of response in ventral visual cortex, and animate items are both rare in standard image sets and among the most memorable (Fig. 2a).
text.formatted: Animacy, for example, is one of the largest dimensions of response in ventral visual cortex, and animate items are both rare in standard image sets and among the most memorable (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref>).

text.text: Any neural measure that distinguishes animate from inanimate stimuli will therefore correlate with memorability across such an image set, even if it contains no information about memory per se.

More generally, neural responses to an image shown in isolation can reflect only how that image relates to the observer's past experience, and wherever the images that are rare in an image set also tend to be rare in that experience, correlations between activity and memorability are expected even if memorability is entirely relational.

Thus, in an emergent memorability account, the success of both artificial models and biological signatures stems not from uncovering fundamental intrinsic properties of memorability that can be decoded from images independent of context, but instead from internalizing the similarity structure of training data and the distinctiveness of images within that similarity structure into the models and readouts of the brain data.
In line with this prediction, the limitations of models become apparent when tested on novel image sets.
Independent benchmarks by Hagen and Espeseth (2023) revealed dramatic performance degradation when ResMem was evaluated across multiple image sets.
text.formatted: Independent benchmarks by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hagen and Espeseth (2023)</ref> revealed dramatic performance degradation when ResMem was evaluated across multiple image sets.

text.text: Variance explained dropped precipitously from approximately 45% on in-distribution data to only 13% on PASCAL-S natural images, 5% on the THINGS object image set, and 2% on object crops, overall representing reductions of 71% to 96% in variance explained in out-of-distribution data.

An item can be distinctive in two senses, either relative to the other items in the experiment (e.g., it is the only tattooed face on the study list or at test), or relative to what an observer has learned over a lifetime (e.g., face tattoos are rare among the faces people have seen).

The first, which we refer to as competitor structure, is what our experiments manipulate, since the items in the experiment determine which stored traces a test item is matched against, and which new items it must be discriminated from.
This alone may be sufficient to explain memorability, as the effects of both study and test manipulations are large and easily flip which items are found to be memorable.
However, one specific factor may depend on the lifetime of experience more so than other aspects of memory.

That is, in global matching models, the rare-feature weighting (e.g., the greater evidence from a matching green mohawk than from matching brown eyes) can be conceived of in multiple ways, and our data do not distinguish between them.

One possibility is that this rare-feature weighting reflects a learned base rate, as typically assumed in REM, where the evidence provided by a match depends on how rare the matching value is in the observer's long-term experience (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: One possibility is that this rare-feature weighting reflects a learned base rate, as typically assumed in REM, where the evidence provided by a match depends on how rare the matching value is in the observer's long-term experience <ref type="bibr">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Another possibility is that rarity that weights some feature matches more is computed relative to the study list, as in hybrid-similarity exemplar models, where matches on distinctive features add to summed similarity (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003).
text.formatted: Another possibility is that rarity that weights some feature matches more is computed relative to the study list, as in hybrid-similarity exemplar models, where matches on distinctive features add to summed similarity <ref type="bibr">(Knapp et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Our data do not distinguish these, as when we defined rarity only by each participant's own study list, this model reproduced the qualitative patterns in our simulations (SI Appendix, Section 3).

A third possibility is that items with common features suffer more interference from memories outside the experiment (i.e., context noise or background noise; Criss & Shiffrin, 2004; Dennis & Humphreys, 2001; Osth & Dennis, 2015).
text.formatted: A third possibility is that items with common features suffer more interference from memories outside the experiment (i.e., context noise or background noise; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Criss & Shiffrin, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dennis & Humphreys, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Osth & Dennis, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This idea has a long history in face recognition in particular, where typical faces draw more false alarms than unusual ones, possibly because they resemble many faces seen over a lifetime (Bartlett et al., 1984; Vokey & Read, 1992).
text.formatted: This idea has a long history in face recognition in particular, where typical faces draw more false alarms than unusual ones, possibly because they resemble many faces seen over a lifetime <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bartlett et al., 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Vokey & Read, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, none of these possibilities amounts to intrinsic memorability.

In each, the weight given to a rare feature is computed from an item's relation to other items, whether those are the items on the list or the items an observer has previously encountered, and in each it enters a recognition decision only together with how it relates to each of the items in the experiment, and only in a way that requires consideration of the relation of the feature to the lures.

As shown in our face experiment, the diagnosticity of a feature match is not the same thing as the memorability of an item, since what a match on a rare feature is worth depends on whether the lures an item must be distinguished from share that feature.

We do not deny that humans, on average, represent more useful features about some items (e.g., faces) than others (e.g., individual blades of grass), and thus are typically better at discriminating faces from novel lures than blades of grass.
That is, people's representational space is not equally split between all items.
However, while memory operates on top of whatever representational structure exists, memory is relational, not intrinsic (just as red is relationally salient, not intrinsically salient).
Nothing in our account requires memory representations to reorganize across contexts.
In our computational models, the same fixed representational space, applied to a different set of items, produces the changes in memorability we report.

Under a relational account, the fact that humans allocate disproportionate representational resources to animate, social stimuli (e.g., "being alive" explained about half of the explainable variance in similarity judgments of images selected to vary in animacy; Jozwik et al., 2022) does not by itself predict that those stimuli will be more or less memorable.
text.formatted: Under a relational account, the fact that humans allocate disproportionate representational resources to animate, social stimuli (e.g., "being alive" explained about half of the explainable variance in similarity judgments of images selected to vary in animacy; <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Jozwik et al., 2022)</ref> does not by itself predict that those stimuli will be more or less memorable.

text.text: Instead, memorability should depend on whether such stimuli are over-or underrepresented in a given image set relative to their footprint in human representational space.
When an image set samples the world in a way that leaves regions of high representational importance sparsely populated, items in those regions become distinctive by default.
This appears to be the case for animate and social categories in standard image sets like THINGS (Hebart et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This appears to be the case for animate and social categories in standard image sets like THINGS <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Representational structure clearly shapes the conditions under which distinctiveness arises, but memory depends on distinctiveness, not on representational structure per se.
Apparent category-level, feature-level and item-level differences in memorability likely reflect differences in distinctiveness masquerading as intrinsic properties.
Our findings raise important questions about what constitutes appropriate image sets for measuring memory.
A practical implication of our emergent memorability account is that there is no such thing as a neutral image set.
Every collection of stimuli has a similarity structure that directly shapes which features will appear memorable and which will not.
Randomly sampling from an image set does not eliminate this structure but inherits it.
This has concrete consequences for how the field uses large image sets.
THINGS was constructed by systematically sampling concrete, picturable nouns from American English.

This is a principled procedure (Hebart et al., 2019), but we suggest that it produces a distribution of object concepts that mismatches human representational space in important ways (Contier et al., 2024; see Fig. 2b).
text.formatted: This is a principled procedure <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2019)</ref>, but we suggest that it produces a distribution of object concepts that mismatches human representational space in important ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Contier et al., 2024</ref>; see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2b</ref>).

text.text: The image set contains many more exemplars of categories like tools than of categories like faces, despite the vastly greater importance of social and animate stimuli in human experience and neural representation (Hebart et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The image set contains many more exemplars of categories like tools than of categories like faces, despite the vastly greater importance of social and animate stimuli in human experience and neural representation <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: What, then, is the ideal image set for measuring memorability?
We argue that there is no such image set.
The first candidate is a memory list that perfectly equates spacing in human representational space.

If items were chosen in proportion to representation, both at study and at test, there would be a lot of things we care about and represent well (e.g., faces) and much less of the things we represent sparsely (e.g., grass blades).
Would memorability still exist in this case?

On the one hand, a face with a rare feature would still be called old more often in such a list, but this would not be memorability, as it would arise only if the lures were not themselves representative in the same way (since a rare lure is itself called old very frequently if it matches items seen in the list; SI Appendix, Fig. S10b).
text.formatted: On the one hand, a face with a rare feature would still be called old more often in such a list, but this would not be memorability, as it would arise only if the lures were not themselves representative in the same way (since a rare lure is itself called old very frequently if it matches items seen in the list; SI Appendix, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S10b</ref>).

text.text: A second is an image set that matches the frequency of items in the world, which would vastly oversample unimportant stimuli like ants and leaves, which matter little to humans and would therefore be confusable and poorly memorable.

And an image set that matches the statistics of human visual experience would still mismatch representation in key ways, devoting far more space to blades of grass and less to large mammals like elephants and zebras than people actually store, leading to unequal memorability for that reason.
A key aspect of the emergent memorability account is in fact that no ground truth memorability can exist outside of the context of a particular image set or list.
A final consideration concerns how memory performance should be measured to assess memorability, regardless of whether it is intrinsic or emergent.

The most common paradigm in the memorability literature is continuous recognition, in which participants view a long stream of images and respond to each one, typically pressing a key when they detect a repeat (e.g., Bainbridge et al., 2013; Isola et al., 2014).
text.formatted: The most common paradigm in the memorability literature is continuous recognition, in which participants view a long stream of images and respond to each one, typically pressing a key when they detect a repeat (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Bainbridge et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Isola et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In the present work, rather than continuous recognition, which gives rise to a heavily biased criterion, we used a more standard study-test procedure with confidence ratings, which allows proper ROC analysis.

Because we did not have any extreme response biases, we did not find major differences between d a and corrected recognition in our data (see SI Appendix, Section 2), and thus focused on corrected recognition to make our work comparable to previous work in this field.
However, this is not a general property of such datasets.
Continuous recognition paradigms, which produce few false alarms, generally mix memory with response bias in ways that are difficult to separate (SI Appendix, Section 2).
Our global matching framework also suggests that hits and false alarm rates may be important to analyze separately rather than collapsed into a single measure when considering memorability.

The model makes distinct predictions for the two, since items that are typical of a well-represented category (say, a common household object in an image set full of common household objects) will generate not only relatively high hit rates, but also high false alarm rates because novel exemplars of that category will match many stored traces.

By contrast, items with rare or unusual features (our face-tattoo example) are predicted to generate high hit rates through a strong self-match likelihood ratio, but may not always lead to high false alarms, as what happens to false alarms depends on the lures.
Over the past two decades, the memorability literature has established that consistency in what people remember is a robust phenomenon.
Although intrinsic memorability is, in principle, difficult to falsify, our findings suggest that the methods typically used to support its existence fall short.
We have argued that this consistency has been systematically misattributed.
Consistency does not require items to have fixed, intrinsic memory properties.
It requires only that the distributional structure shaping what is distinctive remains stable across studies, which it does whenever studies draw from the same image sets.

Thus, consistency and context-dependence are not in conflict: memorability can be both highly consistent within a given experimental tradition and highly mutable when the similarity structure of the stimulus set changes, as our experiments show.
The relational, emergent account we have advanced is grounded in well-established principles of global matching models that have successfully explained a wide range of memory phenomena for decades.
What we have done is apply these principles to the question of memorability, showing that they are sufficient to explain the patterns that have been taken as evidence for something more intrinsic.
This does not close the book on memorability research.
It simply reframes what the most important questions are.

Rather than asking which images are memorable and why, the more productive questions may be: what is the representational structure of the stimulus sets we use, how does that structure shape distinctiveness, how does that depend on study lists vs. test lures, and how can we design experiments that disentangle distributional effects from genuine item-level variation (if such variation exists)?
How can we scale up memorability to the real world once we acknowledge the emergent nature of memorability?
Answering these questions will require new image sets, new experimental designs, and a closer dialogue between the memorability literature and the broader cognitive science of recognition memory.

When false alarms are near floor.
The continuous recognition task that produced the THINGS memorability scores is different.
Its measure is almost certainly not an accurate measure of memory per se.

With a mean false alarm rate of 0.02 across 26,107 images, the published "memorability" score is effectively solely an index of hit rate (r = 0.987, 95% CI [0.987, 0.988]) and not false alarm rate (r = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.07]; Fig. S18c).
text.formatted: With a mean false alarm rate of 0.02 across 26,107 images, the published "memorability" score is effectively solely an index of hit rate (r = 0.987, 95% CI [0.987, 0.988]) and not false alarm rate (r = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.07]; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_25">S18c</ref>).

text.text: An effect of similar items in the study list that acts through false alarms is therefore effectively not at all present in the memorability literature, as criteria are so extreme in this task that it is unknown how strong memory actually is for each item (e.g., how many additional hits could people get before they began really false alarming?).

A hit rate also cannot separate better memory from a greater willingness to say "old", since an image that makes people more inclined to respond "old" will have more hits whether or not it is better remembered, and with false alarms near floor for all images the score has no way to correct for this (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004).

text.text: Thus, we strongly believe future memorability studies should use a more standard study-test design or at minimum ensure participants are reliably above floor on false alarm rates.

text.text: Context manipulation.
The strongest evidence offered for intrinsic memorability is that the rank order of items' memorability is stable across large changes in context.

In particular, Bylinskii et al. (2015) measured memorability for the same target scenes in two very different contexts: within-category (e.g., amusement park images studied alongside other amusement parks) and across-category (amusement park images studied alongside houses, pastures, and mountains).
text.formatted: In particular, <ref type="bibr">Bylinskii et al. (2015)</ref> measured memorability for the same target scenes in two very different contexts: within-category (e.g., amusement park images studied alongside other amusement parks) and across-category (amusement park images studied alongside houses, pastures, and mountains).

text.text: Memorability in the two contexts was similar (Spearman ρ = 0.60 for hit rates), which has been taken to show that memorability reflects properties of the image that are independent of context.

A global matching model with no intrinsic memorability produces the same stability under the same manipulation, because adding many items from the same category makes all of the items in that category harder to remember without causing rank order change in which of them are the most distinctive.
Simulation.
We simulated both experimental contexts in REM to test whether this consistency requires intrinsic memorability.
We generated 21 categories with 300 items each (75 targets, 225 fillers), matching the structure of Bylinskii et al. (2015).

Our REM simulations closely replicated the human findings.

We generated 21 simulated 'scene categories', each containing 300 items (75 targets and 225 fillers), matching the structure of Bylinskii et al. (2015).

text.text: Items were represented as arbitrary 49-d feature vectors with all parameters identical to the REM simulation of Fig. 1: features drawn from a geometric distribution (g = 0.65), encoding probability = 0.3, and correct encoding probability = 0.6.

text.text: To create categorical structure, we designated the first 10 features as category-defining features.
For each category, we generated a category prototype by drawing 10 feature values from the geometric distribution.
All items within that category shared these 10 category-defining feature values, while the remaining 39 features varied independently across items.
We then simulated two experimental contexts corresponding to Bylinskii et al.'s design.
In the within-category simulation, we conducted separate recognition memory experiments for each of the 21 categories.

Consistent with empirical data, we varied the recognition criterion between experiments: within-category simulations used a criterion of 20, while across-category simulations used a criterion of 5 to reflect participants' actual tendencies to adopt a more conservative criterion as items become more similar (e.g., Nosofsky & Kantner, 2006).

text.text: For each simulation run, we randomly sampled 30 targets and 90 fillers from within a single category, encoded them following standard REM procedures, and tested recognition memory against a decision criterion of 20.
In the across-category simulation, we tested the same target items in mixed-category contexts.
For each simulation run, we randomly sampled 30 targets and 90 fillers across all 21 categories and tested recognition memory against a criterion of 5.
For the across-category context, we conducted 1,000 simulation runs.
For the within-category context, we conducted 1,000 simulation runs per category (21,000 total).
This yielded stable memorability estimates (hit rate minus false alarm rate) for each target item.
False alarm rates were computed by testing each target's familiarity signal against separately generated novel lures.
Finally, we again computed summed similarity using the same L2 norm approach described in Section 1.
Mirroring the structure of the simulated memory experiments, in the within-category simulation each item's summed similarity was computed as the negative of the average
Euclidean distance to all other items within its category.
In the across-category simulation, each item's summed similarity was computed as the negative of the average Euclidean distance to all items across all categories.
Adapting REM to continuous recognition.
As noted above, memorability has often been measured with continuous recognition rather than with the study-test lists of Fig. 1.
text.formatted: As noted above, memorability has often been measured with continuous recognition rather than with the study-test lists of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Continuous recognition has no separate phases, since each trial tests the item on screen and is also a new study event.
We adapted REM to run this task trial by trial while keeping its decision rule.
Memory grows during the session.

On each trial the item on screen is compared with all traces stored on earlier trials, using REM's likelihood ratio (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), and the model responds "old" when the average likelihood ratio across those traces exceeds its criterion.
text.formatted: On each trial the item on screen is compared with all traces stored on earlier trials, using REM's likelihood ratio <ref type="bibr">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, and the model responds "old" when the average likelihood ratio across those traces exceeds its criterion.

text.text: After the response, the item is stored as a new trace, whether it was shown for the first time or repeated.
A repeat is therefore judged against a memory that holds its own earlier trace along with all other items stored so far.

Because continuous recognition produces far fewer false alarms than a study-test list, we did not use REM's usual criterion of 1.0 but set it so that the model's false alarm rate matched the participants' rate of 2%.
Because traces were never forgotten, any loss of memory over a session comes from interference among the stored traces.
Simulated THINGS trial sequences.

Each simulated participant followed the trial sequence of one participant in the original THINGS memorability study in terms of old vs. new items (Kramer et al., 2023), taken from the raw trial-level data, with first showings and repeats in the same order and at the same lags.
text.formatted: Each simulated participant followed the trial sequence of one participant in the original THINGS memorability study in terms of old vs. new items <ref type="bibr">(Kramer et al., 2023)</ref>, taken from the raw trial-level data, with first showings and repeats in the same order and at the same lags.

text.text: We used the sequences of 400 participants, with ten simulated participants on each.
Because each distinct image was replaced by an item with REM's generated features, the similarity of the preceding items to each probe arose only by chance.
We ran the model at the standard storage probability (0.30) and at a higher one (0.75) that brings its overall d′ close to participants'.
As in the data, the same item was remembered less well when the items shown before it were more similar (Fig. S5).
text.formatted: As in the data, the same item was remembered less well when the items shown before it were more similar (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">S5</ref>).

text.text: In particular, d′ fell by 0.51 in the data and by 0.63 and 1.12 in the model (depending on its parameters; Spearman ρ = -1.00 to -0.98), and false alarms more than doubled in the data and in the standard model and rose tenfold at the higher storage probability (ρ = 0.98 to 1.00).
At the higher storage probability the measured criterion also became more liberal with similar preceding items, as in the data (ρ = -1.00; data, ρ = -0.79).

Because the model's threshold is fixed, this apparent shift is not a criterion shift per se but reflects a stronger memory signal for new items that resemble recent ones, which, when analyzed post hoc, can falsely appear to be a criterion shift.
Thus, a global matching model produces the context cost of the continuous recognition task, and an apparent criterion shift, with no item-intrinsic memorability and no strategic adjustment.
The same item on crowded and uncrowded lists.
Global matching models predict that an item's memorability depends on the items it is studied with, as well as the lures it is tested against.
To test this directly in the model, we held each item fixed and changed only the other items on its 40-item study list, at the parameter values of Fig. 1.
text.formatted: To test this directly in the model, we held each item fixed and changed only the other items on its 40-item study list, at the parameter values of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: On random lists, close neighbors appeared by chance.
On designed lists, we placed 16 of an item's close neighbors on its list and used its nearest neighbor, never studied, as its lure.
Crowded lists raised both hits and false alarms, but raised false alarms more (designed lists: hits +0.08, 95% CI [0.07, 0.09]; false alarms +0.11, 95% CI [0.10, 0.12]).
Thus, d′ fell (Fig. S6), by 0.07 (95% CI [0.06, 0.09]) on random lists and by 0.13 (95% CI [0.09, 0.17]) on designed lists.
text.formatted: Thus, d′ fell (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_11">S6</ref>), by 0.07 (95% CI [0.06, 0.09]) on random lists and by 0.13 (95% CI [0.09, 0.17]) on designed lists.

text.text: Because both rates rose together, corrected recognition registered little of this cost.
In the model, the same item is remembered less well when its list makes it less distinctive.
The cost is clearest in d′, which does not depend on the overall rate of "old" responses.
REM with measured features.
In standard REM, an item is a list of features whose values are drawn at random from a geometric distribution.
Thus, which items resemble each other is decided by chance.

To test whether the crowding effects depend on that generated structure, we made each simulated item a THINGS concept (Hebart et al., 2019), such that its features were the concept's 49 SPoSE values (Hebart et al., 2020), dimensions derived from people's choices of the odd one out among three objects (e.g., how animal-related or food-related a concept is).
text.formatted: To test whether the crowding effects depend on that generated structure, we made each simulated item a THINGS concept <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2019)</ref>, such that its features were the concept's 49 SPoSE values <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020)</ref>, dimensions derived from people's choices of the odd one out among three objects (e.g., how animal-related or food-related a concept is).

text.text: Thus, human similarity judgments, rather than the simulation, determined which items were similar and which were distinctive (results in Fig. S7).
text.formatted: Thus, human similarity judgments, rather than the simulation, determined which items were similar and which were distinctive (results in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">S7</ref>).

text.text: Because SPoSE values are continuous rather than discrete like REM's, the model kept REM's likelihood ratio but changed how the rarity of a value is judged and how a probe value is matched to a stored one.
The rarity of a feature value was judged against the distribution of that feature across the 1,600 concepts.
Thus, agreeing on a value that few concepts share counts for more than agreeing on a common one, as in REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997).
text.formatted: Thus, agreeing on a value that few concepts share counts for more than agreeing on a common one, as in REM <ref type="bibr">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Because two continuous values never match exactly, the model adds one parameter, retention noise.
A correctly stored feature is set to the studied value plus Gaussian noise, with a standard deviation set as a fraction of that feature's spread across concepts.
A probe value then counts as evidence for a trace according to how close it falls to the stored value under that noise, relative to how common the value is among all concepts.
The study and test design and the storage and copy parameters were identical to those in Fig. 1, and we report results at several noise levels rather than fitting the noise.
text.formatted: The study and test design and the storage and copy parameters were identical to those in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, and we report results at several noise levels rather than fitting the noise.

text.text: We find, as expected, that concepts that sit close to their 20 nearest neighbors were less memorable (ρ = -0.52 to -0.44, all p < 0.001, n = 1,600 concepts; -0.55 with REM's generated features in the run of Fig. 1; Section 4 gives the relationship at every scale), and a concept studied with its 16 closest neighbors lost 0.34 to 0.44 in d′, more than with REM's generated features (0.13), because false alarms to its nearest neighbor rose (Fig. S7).
text.formatted: We find, as expected, that concepts that sit close to their 20 nearest neighbors were less memorable (ρ = -0.52 to -0.44, all p < 0.001, n = 1,600 concepts; -0.55 with REM's generated features in the run of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>; Section 4 gives the relationship at every scale), and a concept studied with its 16 closest neighbors lost 0.34 to 0.44 in d′, more than with REM's generated features (0.13), because false alarms to its nearest neighbor rose (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">S7</ref>).

text.text: Both signatures of the main-text simulations therefore arise when distinctiveness comes from the measured similarity structure of THINGS concepts.
The model.
REM is one of many global matching models.

To test whether our simulation results depend on REM's likelihood ratio and use of world rarity to weight rare features, we replaced it with a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), keeping the generated features, encoding and lists of Fig. 1.
text.formatted: To test whether our simulation results depend on REM's likelihood ratio and use of world rarity to weight rare features, we replaced it with a hybrid-similarity exemplar model <ref type="bibr">(Knapp et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>, keeping the generated features, encoding and lists of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: In this model, familiarity is the summed similarity of the probe to the stored traces.

The similarity of a probe to a trace is exp(-c•d) × exp(γ•m), where d is the Euclidean distance between them over the features the trace stored and m is the number of stored features on which they share a distinctive value.
We defined a feature value as distinctive when three or fewer of the 40 items on that simulated participant's own study list had it.
Thus, rarity was defined by the study list alone and not by a long-term base rate or world rarity.
We used γ = 2 and a fixed criterion at a false alarm rate of 0.15, without fitting either.
The similarity width c was set to the value, among nine candidates, that brought overall d′ closest to REM's (c = 1.42 at γ = 2 and 2.26 at γ = 0).
Simulation results.
The model reproduced the qualitative pattern of all three simulation results.
Isolated items were more memorable (ρ = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.36, -0.27], compared with -0.61 in REM at the Fig. 1 values, in the run of Fig. S3; Fig. S8a).

text.text: On designed lists, studying 16 of an item's close neighbors raised its hits by 0.06 (95% CI [0.04, 0.07]) and false alarms to its nearest neighbor by 0.13 (95% CI [0.12, 0.14]), and d′ fell by 0.26 (95% CI [0.22, 0.29], n = 200 critical items; Fig. S8b and c).

(2015) context manipulation, an item's memorability within its category predicted its memorability across categories (ρ = 0.48, 95% CI [0.44, 0.52], n = 1,575 targets; positive in all 19 settings of a sweep over criteria, category structure and model parameters, ρ = 0.15 to 0.74).

text.text: The effects are not matched in size to REM's, since overall accuracy was lower in this model (d′ of 0.82, and 0.66 in the GCM, compared with 1.61).
The advantage for isolated items held in 25 of 26 settings of a parameter sweep (ρ = -0.47 to +0.01) and depended on the weight given to rare matches.

With γ = 0, which is the generalized context model (Nosofsky, 1986), not the hybrid version, the listcontext cost remained but isolated items were no longer more memorable (ρ = +0.26, 95% CI [0.22, 0.31]).

text.text: This suggests that weighting distinctive features more is key to explaining memorability through crowding, although our simulations do not determine the extent to which this weighting must be based on world rarity (as in REM) vs. list rarity (as in the Hybrid-GCM model).

The analyses in the main text and elsewhere in this appendix measure how crowded an item is in several ways, depending on what kind of model is used and what the shape of the data is (e.g., discrete vs. continuous).

Here we apply a unified measure to each dataset and vary how local it is (e.g., how much the nearest items contribute vs. all items), reporting hits, false alarms and d′ separately to show robustness and the patterns of hits and false alarms.
Our measure.

For each item, we defined crowding as the mean of exp(-d/τ) over the other items, where d is 1 minus the Pearson correlation of two concepts' SPoSE vectors, or the Euclidean distance between two simulated items divided by its median where appropriate.
When τ is small (e.g., τ = 0.05), only an item's nearest neighbors contribute.
As τ grows, all items in the set count more equally, and in the limit crowding is the mean similarity to the whole set.
Crowding was computed at τ = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 1 and in the all-items limit, in seven datasets.

These were the REM simulation of Fig. 1, the REM model on SPoSE features of Fig. S7, the hybrid model with rarity computed from the study list of Fig. S8, the original THINGS memorability data (concept hit rates on target repeats and false-alarm rates on first showings, computed from the trial records of Kramer et al., 2023), and the maintained, changed and reduced image sets.
text.formatted: These were the REM simulation of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, the REM model on SPoSE features of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_12">S7</ref>, the hybrid model with rarity computed from the study list of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S8</ref>, the original THINGS memorability data (concept hit rates on target repeats and false-alarm rates on first showings, computed from the trial records of <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al., 2023)</ref>, and the maintained, changed and reduced image sets.

text.text: Crowding raises false alarms in all datasets and at all scales.

Crowded items were falsely recognized more often in all seven datasets at every value of τ (Fig. S9a; Spearman ρ from 0.11 to 0.75), and in the image sets this held within higher-level categories as well (ρ = 0.14 to 0.29 in the maintained and changed sets).
text.formatted: Crowded items were falsely recognized more often in all seven datasets at every value of τ (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">S9a</ref>; Spearman ρ from 0.11 to 0.75), and in the image sets this held within higher-level categories as well (ρ = 0.14 to 0.29 in the maintained and changed sets).

text.text: Global matching models predict exactly this, because a new item that resembles many studied items produces a strong match to them.
Hits reflect two influences that crowding pulls in opposite directions.
In global matching models, a probe that resembles many stored items receives extra matches, which raises both hits and false alarms.
Most of these models also weight a match by how rare the matching features are, which raises hits for items with rare features.

REM computes that rarity against the observer's lifetime experience (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), whereas hybrid-similarity models compute it against the items on the study list (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003).
text.formatted: REM computes that rarity against the observer's lifetime experience <ref type="bibr">(Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997)</ref>, whereas hybrid-similarity models compute it against the items on the study list <ref type="bibr">(Knapp et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, whereas false alarms should depend mainly on the first influence (and indeed, they rose with crowding at all scales), hits depend on the balance between the two.
When crowding also makes an item's features common, as it does in REM, crowded items draw fewer hits.
In the hybrid model at the settings of Fig. S8, the extra matches outweigh the bonus for rare features, and crowded items draw more hits (Fig. S9b).
text.formatted: In the hybrid model at the settings of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S8</ref>, the extra matches outweigh the bonus for rare features, and crowded items draw more hits (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_14">S9b</ref>).

text.text: The balance between the two influences therefore decides the direction of the hit effect.
In people the hit effect was small and varied in sign across datasets and scales.

When crowding changed for a concept between image sets, its false alarms rose (ρ = 0.14 and 0.45), while its hits stayed the same (ρ = -0.01) or fell (ρ = -0.34), and the same image after a more similar stream drew more false alarms and no more hits (Fig. S15).
text.formatted: When crowding changed for a concept between image sets, its false alarms rose (ρ = 0.14 and 0.45), while its hits stayed the same (ρ = -0.01) or fell (ρ = -0.34), and the same image after a more similar stream drew more false alarms and no more hits (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_21">S15</ref>).

text.text: Crowding lowers d′ at all scales.

Because false alarms rose more than hits, even when hits went up, d′ fell with crowding in all datasets (Fig. S9c), from -0.13 to -0.20 in THINGS, -0.13 to -0.48 in the maintained set, -0.45 to -0.48 in the changed set and -0.04 to -0.17 in the reduced set, compared with -0.17 to -0.63 in the three models.

text.text: Corrected recognition can reverse the sign.

Because false alarms in the THINGS task are near floor (Section 2) and nearest-neighbor crowding goes with more hits across THINGS concepts, corrected recognition can rise with crowding even though d′ falls.
This is a pitfall of the inability to criterion-correct memory from this task.
For example, the feature-level analysis of Fig. 2a shows this (Table S2).
text.formatted: For example, the feature-level analysis of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">2a</ref> shows this (Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Measured with d′, features that predict crowding predict poorer memory at all scales, whereas measured with corrected recognition the relationship reverses for the most local measures.
The same analysis in the changed set holds at all scales with either measure, and in the maintained set at all scales except the most local one.

Crowding measured over each THINGS concept's five nearest concepts in the deep-network spaces of Section 7 shows the same pattern, with more crowded concepts receiving more false alarms (ρ = 0.33), slightly more hits (ρ = 0.07) and lower d′ (ρ = -0.18).
Thus, crowding did not predict corrected recognition (ρ = 0.03, p = 0.23).

The reduced set.
The reduced set was built to equalize the summed similarity of Fig. 2, and it halved the spread of crowding measured over the whole set (SD ratio, reduced to maintained, 0.51 in the all-items limit).

This suggests that the reduction of Fig. 2h is best described as a reduction in how much concepts differ in their similarity to the set as a whole.

text.text: The inversion experiment changed what each item was studied alongside without changing the test structure.
However, global matching models also predict that what an item is tested against should be key to its memorability.
Our second experiment tests this prediction with faces, focusing on a version of the tattoo example in the main text.
In particular, we held the studied faces fixed and changed only whether a new face at test contained the same rare feature.
Participants studied 50 synthetic faces (N = 100, preregistered; Methods below).
Six of the studied faces had a feature that is rare in everyday life: an electric-green mohawk, a long forked beard, and four combinations of makeup, ink, piercings and eyewear.
Each of these features was carried by a pair of different people (e.g., two different people with the mohawk).
One member of each pair was studied, chosen at random for each participant, and the other could appear at test as a lure with the same feature.
Our manipulation was therefore at the level of the feature rather than the face.
A rare feature appeared at test on the face that had been studied, and on a new face that had not.
The rest of the test was ordinary faces, half of them studied and half new.
If a rare feature makes a face intrinsically memorable, it should improve memory overall.
If memorability is relational relative to the test items, not only the study items, the feature should help only when no new face at test also has it.
We found that studied faces with a rare feature were called old more often than ordinary studied faces (0.90 vs.

text.text: However, new faces with a rare feature were also called old more often, relative to new faces with no rare feature, and in fact the feature inflated false alarms further than it inflated hits (false alarms 0.59 vs.
0.41, t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001; increase in false alarms vs. increase in hits, +0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033).

text.text: Thus, consistent with global matching models, matching on a rare feature is strong evidence that a face was studied, but this is true whether or not the rest of the face matches.
Thus, a rare face tested against a new face with the same feature was no more discriminable than an ordinary face (Fig. S10c).
text.formatted: Thus, a rare face tested against a new face with the same feature was no more discriminable than an ordinary face (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S10c</ref>).

text.text: Rare faces led to d a = 1.67 (95% CI [1.47, 1.89]) against unrelated new faces and 1.00 (95% CI [0.75, 1.25]) against new faces with their feature, identical to the discriminability of ordinary faces against unrelated new faces (1.00, 95% CI [0.90, 1.11]).

Thus, a rare feature made a face more memorable than an ordinary one only if no new face had the same feature, and if new faces shared the same feature, the rare feature actually made faces slightly less memorable than an ordinary face (a drop of 0.18, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001, dz = 0.59, and a shortfall of 0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033, dz = 0.22; Fig. S12a).

text.text: Comparing each face against itself across participants, as usual in memorability work, the rare faces were no more memorable than the ordinary ones (hit minus false-alarm rate 0.33 against 0.38; d′ 1.12 against 1.10), since their extra hits (0.90 against 0.79) were matched by extra false alarms (0.57 against 0.41).
Thus, a rare feature does provide a strong match signal, but that is not the same thing as being intrinsically memorable.
The feature's effect on memorability depends on the set the face is judged in.
It gives a large advantage when no other face has the feature, and loses that advantage as soon as one does.

Methods.
This experiment was preregistered (AsPredicted #311640).
Stimuli were photorealistic synthetic faces generated with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model, each a front-facing studio portrait with a neutral expression on a plain gray background.
Twelve faces formed six pairs.

The two members of a pair were different people of the same age band, sex and race who had the same rare feature (an electric-green mohawk, a long forked beard, or an unusual combination of makeup, facial ink, piercings or eyewear).
The other 59 faces were ordinary faces with none of these features.

Each participant studied 50 faces (one randomly chosen member of each rare-feature pair and 44 ordinary faces) for 3 s each with a 500 ms interstimulus interval, pressing the space bar whenever a face repeated immediately (six ordinary faces that were never tested repeated in this way).
After 60 s of arithmetic, they completed 36 old/new recognition trials, each followed by a four-point confidence rating.
Three rare-feature pairs were tested with the studied face and three with the unstudied member of the pair, along with 15 studied and 15 unstudied ordinary faces.

Memorability (Fig. S12a) was corrected recognition computed for each participant, with the false alarm rate taken either from unstudied ordinary faces or from the unstudied members of the rare-feature pairs, and conditions were compared with paired t-tests.
text.formatted: Memorability (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_17">S12a</ref>) was corrected recognition computed for each participant, with the false alarm rate taken either from unstudied ordinary faces or from the unstudied members of the rare-feature pairs, and conditions were compared with paired t-tests.

text.text: Participants.

The final sample was the first 100 participants, recruited online through Prolific, who passed the preregistered exclusion rule (at least 4 of the 6 repeats detected and no more than 5 presses to non-repeated faces during study); 11 additional participants were run and excluded under this rule.
Predictions made before data collection.

text.text: On neither measure does a rare feature give a face an advantage.
Instead, how memorable a face looks depends on what it is tested against.
The THINGS analyses rest on one image set of objects and on one embedding of 49 features.
Here we test whether the link between distinctiveness and memorability depends on either choice.
Summed similarity in deep-network spaces.

We embedded all released images of a face image set (Bainbridge et al., 2013) and a scene image set (Isola et al., 2011), unscored fillers included, in the 14 deep-network spaces of Section 7, and computed each scored image's summed similarity to the whole set, with all features weighted equally or with feature weights fitted on other images of the same image set.

SPoSE refits.
The 49 SPoSE features are the ones published by Hebart et al. (2020) and that Kramer et al. (2023) analyzed memorability with respect to, and we used them as published.

text.text: SPoSE (Zheng et al., 2019) learns these features directly from people's odd-one-out choices.

text.text: Each concept receives a non-negative weight on each candidate feature, and the similarity of two concepts is the overlap of their weights.
The weights are adjusted until the model predicts which object people picked as the odd one out in each set of three.
A sparsity penalty pushes features the choices do not need toward zero, and features left with no substantial weight on any concept are removed.
The number of features is therefore not chosen in advance.
It depends on the penalty and on the amount of data (e.g., the larger THINGS-data release yields 66 features; Hebart et al., 2023).

text.text: To test whether our results depend on this number, we refit SPoSE from scratch to the raw THINGS-data choices, starting from 100 candidate features, at a range of penalty strengths, then recomputed summed similarity in each refit's own features and repeated the analyses.

In all refits in which the penalty removed features, leaving between 6 and 81, the least distinctive features were again the least memorable (r = -0.81 to -0.50 across the 14 refits, p < 0.01 with 17 or more features and p = 0.053 with 6, compared with -0.61, 95% CI [-0.68, -0.51], for the published embedding; Fig. S14), and the four image-set correlations of Fig. 2d to g that use SPoSE features kept their signs.

text.text: The trial-level records of the original memorability study with THINGS (Kramer et al., 2023) allow a direct test of context.
text.formatted: The trial-level records of the original memorability study with THINGS <ref type="bibr">(Kramer et al., 2023)</ref> allow a direct test of context.

text.text: Because each participant in continuous recognition sees a different stream, the same image appears after preceding images that are sometimes similar to it and sometimes not.
Comparing an image with itself across these streams holds everything about the image constant and varies only its context.
Within-image context.

For each trial we measured how similar the preceding stream was to the probe (the mean SPoSE similarity of the most similar images already shown) and ranked each image's trials into bins by that similarity, so that all bins hold the same images.

Across bins, d′ fell at each step, a decline of 0.51 (95% CI [0.48, 0.54], Spearman ρ = -1.00; Fig. S15a), 1.34 times the standard deviation of d′ across images; hits fell and false alarms more than doubled.

text.text: Notably, Bainbridge (2026), analyzing the same trials, found that an image's mean similarity to all preceding images explained little variance in hits once each image's memorability was included.
That memorability score is the image's average performance across contexts, and so already includes the average effect of context.
Comparing the same image across its own contexts, as here, measures the effect directly without removing the variance from contexts first, and finds a large and reliable effect.
Feature similarity and category membership.
Feature similarity, more than shared category membership, accounted for this effect.

With the image held constant, crowding of the preceding stream in SPoSE predicted false alarms 4.6 times (95% CI [2.8, 12.0]) more strongly than the number of preceding items from the probe's higher-level category entered alongside it.
Close competitors are also the most common case in this study.

Of first showings after at least 20 preceding items, only 7.8% arrive with no item of the probe's higher-level category already shown, and 62% of a concept's ten nearest SPoSE neighbors belong to its own category, compared with 4% by chance.
Most images in the memorability study were therefore judged after items from their own category, the items most likely to be their near neighbors.

Because SPoSE is built from human similarity judgments, the context effect of Fig. S15 could in theory come from those judgments rather than from the images.

The main text tests whether memorability is relational in three experiments: the memorability inversion experiment (Fig. 1c), the rare-feature face experiment (Fig. S10; Section 5) and the image set experiments (Fig. 2).

We adjusted only two settings, the noise on stored features and the threshold for responding "old".
We chose them to match our participants' overall false alarm rate and to come close to their overall hit rate.
No parameters were fit to individual items.
Any difference the model shows between items therefore comes only from how similar each item was to the other items on its lists (discounting feature values common in THINGS).
Thus, its item-by-item results are predictions.

text.text: A model whose only information about an item is its similarity to the other items, with no parameter fitted to any item, therefore reproduces the inversion and predicts the direction of the change in memory for the same image between sets.
Hits and false alarms in the inversion experiment.

A similar item on the study list could lower an item's memorability in two ways: by making the studied item harder to recognize, which lowers hits, or by making the item look studied when it was not, which raises false alarms.
In the memorability inversion experiment each critical item was studied by some participants and was an unstudied lure for the others, and thus has both a hit rate and a false alarm rate.

As the number of similar items on the study list rose from 0 to 8, false alarms to the critical items rose from 0.05 to 0.57 (item-wise Spearman ρ = 0.72, 95% CI [0.50, 0.85], p < 0.001) and d′ fell (ρ = -0.49, 95% CI [-0.75, -0.17], p < 0.01; Fig. S18a and b).

text.text: This rise follows from the design, because the items given more similar items were the more memorable ones in THINGS, and so their higher hit rates reflect which items were chosen rather than the manipulation.

This suggests that a close competitor on the study list acts mainly by making a new item look old, likely at least in part because participants cannot know in advance of seeing a given lure what criterion to set for a particular image.

If participants knew they were in a study where "twins" would be present and they had to discriminate twin A from twin B, for example, they would likely set a much higher criterion than if they did not expect such twins until they appeared at test.
In the image set experiments false alarms also contributed most of the same-image change in d′ (0.20, 95% CI [0.17, 0.23], of the 0.28; Fig. S17c).

text.text: Methods
Items were represented as vectors of 49 features, with each feature value drawn from a geometric distribution (with parameter g = 0.65), resulting in integer values starting from 1.

During encoding, each feature was stored with a probability of 0.3, and if stored, was encoded correctly with a probability of 0.6 (otherwise encoded as a random value drawn from the same geometric distribution).
These values differ from the standard values of Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997; 20 features, g = 0.40, and a probability of correct encoding of 0.70).
text.formatted: These values differ from the standard values of <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997</ref>; 20 features, g = 0.40, and a probability of correct encoding of 0.70).

text.text: At those standard values the relationship between distinctiveness and memorability was similar (ρ = -0.52, 95% CI [-0.56, -0.49], rather than -0.55).
It also held across a wide range of other parameter values (Section 3).
We generated a set of 1,600 simulated items to serve as our simulated image set (the same size as the image sets in our behavioral experiments).
To mimic typical memorability experimental conditions, including those in our behavioral experiments, we then conducted 10,000 independently simulated recognition memory experiments.
Each simulation studied 40 items.
Recognition was then tested on 20 randomly chosen studied items plus 20 additional lures drawn from the 1,600-item set.
Across the 10,000 simulations, each item served as both a studied probe and a lure probe in different runs, allowing per-item hit and false-alarm rates to be estimated.
Recognition decisions followed standard REM likelihood ratio procedures.

For each test item, familiarity was calculated by comparing the test item against all stored memory traces (global matching) vs. the likelihood of these same features being stored if the item was not seen (defined as the generative distribution of items, the geometric distribution).
The overall familiarity signal was then computed as the mean likelihood ratio across all stored traces.
Recognition responses were determined by comparing this familiarity signal to a fixed criterion of 1.0.

For each item across all simulation runs, we calculated hit rate (proportion of correct "old" responses when studied) and false alarm rate (proportion of incorrect "old" responses when unstudied), with memorability operationalized as corrected recognition (hit rate minus false alarm rate).
For each item, we also approximated its distinctiveness in the feature space by computing an approximation of the summed similarity of it to all other items.
We did this by calculating the average Euclidean distance to all other items in the image set in the 49-d feature space.
Euclidean distance between two items was computed as the L2 norm of the difference between their feature vectors.

This measure quantified each item's distance from other items, with larger values indicating greater distinctiveness (Fig. 1 uses the inverse of distance as summed similarity, so that larger values there mean more crowded).
text.formatted: This measure quantified each item's distance from other items, with larger values indicating greater distinctiveness (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref> uses the inverse of distance as summed similarity, so that larger values there mean more crowded).

text.text: Note that unlike the model, this distance metric does not take into account that some features are more rare and thus more informative, nor does it take into account that only items with many overlapping features (not just a few) will give rise to confusable memory signals.
It therefore provides only an approximation of the decision rule of the model, but one that can be easily applied to other realistic items in realistic feature spaces.
Inversion Experiment.

For each of the 8 study/test blocks, five critical items were selected from the THINGS image set spanning different memorability levels based on Kramer et al. (2023) scores: one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins, giving 40 total items stratified across these memorability bins.
text.formatted: For each of the 8 study/test blocks, five critical items were selected from the THINGS image set spanning different memorability levels based on <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al. (2023)</ref> scores: one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins, giving 40 total items stratified across these memorability bins.

text.text: We systematically manipulated each critical item's distinctiveness by varying the number of similar context items in study lists, with the number assigned based on each critical item's original memorability bin: 8 similar items for the top 20% (most memorable), 4 for the 60-80% bin, 2 for the 40-60% bin, 1 for the 20-40% bin, and 0 for the bottom 20% (least memorable).

Because we needed item-wise similarity metrics to select these (which are not available for THINGS from any source based on human judgments), item similarity was computed using representational dissimilarity matrices derived from an average across the 4 RDMs derived from ResNet18, VGG16, AlexNet and CLIP, in each case using the highest layer before the output layer.

Each study list contained 40 images: 35 controlled context items (15 similar items distributed across the 5 critical items as described above, plus 20 additional dissimilar exemplars), and 5 additional items selected from the critical items and maximally dissimilar fillers to maintain consistent list length.
Participants performed 8 blocks of study and test.
Participants were told to memorize the images for a later memory test.
Each studied image was shown for 500 ms with an 800 ms interstimulus interval.

In each block participants studied a sequential stream of 40 images, then completed 10 consecutive recognition trials (testing all 5 critical items and all 5 maximally dissimilar items, with old/new status determined by whether each item had appeared in the study stream) judging whether each image was 'old' or 'new' using a 6-point confidence scale.
Whether each tested item was old or new was varied across participants, so that each critical item served as both a studied item and a lure across the sample.
Memorability for each critical item was calculated as corrected recognition, then compared to original Kramer et al. (2023) rankings to assess ranking inversion.

text.text: We constructed representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) over all THINGS concepts for humans (Hebart et al., 2020) and monkeys (Papale et al., 2025).

We derived a behavioral similarity RDM from the large-scale THINGS similarity dataset (Hebart et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We derived a behavioral similarity RDM from the large-scale THINGS similarity dataset <ref type="bibr">(Hebart et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This dataset provides human behavioral judgments summarized as 49-dimensional SPoSE embeddings for each of the 1,854 object concepts.
We treated each embedding as a feature vector and computed pairwise dissimilarities using 1 -Pearson correlation, yielding a symmetric 1,854 × 1,854 RDM.
Concept-level memorability values were then attached by aligning each concept to Kramer et al.'s memorability scores.
In parallel, we constructed an RDM from the THINGS Ventral Stream Spiking Dataset (Papale et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In parallel, we constructed an RDM from the THINGS Ventral Stream Spiking Dataset <ref type="bibr">(Papale et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For each concept, multi-unit spiking responses from macaque IT were reduced to a 49-dimensional feature space using principal component analysis to make them comparable to the SPoSE embeddings.
These 49 components captured nearly all (85%) of the variance in these responses.
As in the human case, we then computed pairwise dissimilarities as 1 -Pearson correlation, yielding a concept-level RDM structurally matched to the human space.
For both human and monkey spaces, we derived a categoryweighted dissimilarity measure for each concept.
To do this, we took the dissimilarity of each concept to all others in the RDM.

These dissimilarities were then weighted by the relative prevalence of each comparison concept's category (i.e., concepts that contained more exemplars contributed proportionally more, to match the memory experiments where generally items are chosen randomly without respect to the concept they belong to).

Because we would not expect items that overlap very little to have much impact on the memory of an item, and would expect a disproportionate amount of interference to arise from very similar items (in line with nearly all global matching models of memory: Nosofsky, 1991; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997;  and other work on how representational distance relates to memory confusability: e.g., Nosofsky, 1992; Schurgin et al., 2020; Shepard, 1987), we used a previously used Gaussian transformation of distance to similarity (Nosofsky, 1992).
text.formatted: Because we would not expect items that overlap very little to have much impact on the memory of an item, and would expect a disproportionate amount of interference to arise from very similar items (in line with nearly all global matching models of memory: <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Nosofsky, 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> and other work on how representational distance relates to memory confusability: e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Nosofsky, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Schurgin et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Shepard, 1987)</ref>, we used a previously used Gaussian transformation of distance to similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Nosofsky, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, the weighted dissimilarities were transformed using a Gaussian kernel centered at minimum dissimilarity (mean = 0, SD = 2) and, because the dissimilarities run only from 0 to 2, this kernel weights all concepts nearly equally, so the measure indexes how close a concept is to the image set as a whole rather than to its nearest neighbors (Section 4 applies one crowding measure, varied from nearest neighbors to the whole set, to every image set in the paper).
This produced a single weighted similarity score for each concept, which we use throughout the paper to relate representational structure to memorability.
Maintained Image Set.
The maintained image set was designed to preserve the original THINGS image set structure by maintaining natural feature-similarity relationships.
For each concept, we calculated a representativeness score based on how well it matched the original correlation pattern between features and similarity.

The representativeness score for each concept was the sum across all of the feature values multiplied by the sign of that feature's correlation with similarity, weighted by the squared magnitude of the correlation.

These scores were normalized to create a probability distribution, and 1,600 concepts were sampled with replacement based on these probabilities, ensuring the image set preserved the original representational structure.
If a concept was sampled more than once, a distinct image from that concept was added to the image set.
The changed image set systematically inverted which regions of the fixed feature space were densely sampled through a two-stage process.
We first identified features positively and negatively correlated with memorability in the original image set.
We then computed concept scores by subtracting weighted positive feature values and adding weighted negative feature values (weighted by squared correlation coefficients).

From the top 500 scoring concepts (those high on "non-memorable" features), we selected 160 concepts using a greedy algorithm that maximized dissimilarity by starting with the highest scoring concept and iteratively adding concepts with minimum average similarity to already selected items.
This created a sparse sampling of typically non-memorable concepts.
We then selected 1,440 additional concepts from those scoring high on positive memorability features, sampled with probability proportional to their squared positive scores.

This oversampling of typically memorable concepts combined with sparse sampling of typically non-memorable concepts changed the distribution of concepts across the feature space in the direction of inverting the feature relationships to memorability.
The reduced image set was constructed to reduce correlations between image features and weighted similarity across concepts using an optimization procedure.
We tested 500 different exponential transformations of memorabilitypredicting feature scores with exponents ranging from 0.01 to 0.5 (in 0.01 increments, replicated 10 times each).
For each transformation, concept scores were normalized from 0 to 1, raised to the test exponent, and used as sampling probabilities for selecting 1,600 concepts with replacement.
For each candidate image set, we computed Spearman correlations between all 49 feature dimensions and weighted similarity values (computed as above).
The composite score was calculated as the sum of the mean of the correlations and the maximum correlation.
The final image set was selected based on the lowest composite score.

measures are inherently noisy, limiting the upper bound of what could be explained by an emergent account in these data.
In particular, human ratings reflect entire categories (what Hebart et al. call 'concepts') rather than specific images, meaning in those ratings we lack good estimates of within-concept variability.
Similarly, monkeys are not humans and monkey visual processing regions capture only one component of the full representational space underlying memory.
Nonetheless, these representational spaces can provide complementary tools for examining how distinctiveness within representational space shapes what we remember.

The final sample consisted of 450 participants across the three image sets: 150 participants in the maintained image set, 150 participants in the changed image set, and 150 participants in the reduced image set, all of whom were recruited from UC San Diego and took part in this study in exchange for course credit.

Across all 3 stimulus set experiments, 152 additional participants were excluded based on the above criteria.Experiments were run online and completed on participants' personal devices.Recognition Memory Task.
All 3 image set experiments used identical recognition memory procedures.
Each participant completed 16 study/test blocks.
In each block, they viewed a study list of 40 images, then completed 40 recognition test trials (20 old, 20 new) judging each as 'old' or 'new' on a 6-point confidence scale.
Participants were told to memorize the images for a later memory test.
Each studied image was shown for 1,000 ms with an 800 ms interstimulus interval.The 20 old items were a subset of the 40 studied images.
The 20 new items were drawn at random from the same image set as the studied images.
Thus, both the studied items and the lures were random samples of the image set, as in standard memorability studies.
Corrected recognition (CR), calculated as hit rate minus false alarm rate, served as the primary memory measure across all experiments.
